p.seg: The First
"Three Poems in Reflection"
Heaven and Earth are full of harmonious energy,
the prime essence shifts with the ages.
Pure Yang shines with brightness,
gentle winds move in harmony.
The bright sun illuminates the sky,
sweet dew spreads over the universe.
Dense and flourishing are the tall pines,
how graceful the long-ranked chǔ trees.
Grass insects cry mournfully,
the cānggēng birds shake their wings.
Stirred by the times, my thoughts arise,
raising my head, I long and linger.
How resplendent the imperial court,
with Yī Héng serving as the assistant.
My talent does not equal that of a true scholar,
my capacity is not that of one versed in war.
So to Yuán and Xiāng Rivers I shall go,
entrusting my fate to a fisherman.
Leisurely!
At ease!
Thus I dwell, thus I rest.
The Second
The moon is bright, the stars are few,
sky high, the air is cold.
Osmanthus banners and emerald pennants,
pendants of jade ring with the luán bird's chime.
Washing my tassels in fine spring water,
I wear robes of huì and lán.
Longing to follow the two maidens,
and go to the Xiāng and Yuán Rivers.
Their spirits are subtle, hearing is slight,
who can look upon their jade-like faces?
Brilliant are the spring blossoms,
green leaves hold vermilion within.
The sun and moon pass away,
how I pity your flourishing beauty!
The Third
The clear wind is solemn and chill,
the long night stretches on and on.
Sighing and singing, grieving within,
sleeping alone, I wake and give voice.
Faced with my cup, I beat my breast,
before food, I forget to eat.
The world holds no xuāncǎo now,
thus I cry with sorrow.
Calling birds seek companions,
the "Gǔ Fēng" censures faults.
Chónghuá was employed in office,
the Emperor commanded Kǎi and Yuán.
Bào Zǐ tilted his carriage cover,
Zhòng Fù aided Huán.
On the riverbank, I sigh for Yú,
how dare I not look up to Yán!
My will holds to bright standards,
I do not envy those who brush their hats for favors.
What is my heart?
Its fragrance is like lán.
The First
"Eighty-Two Poems in Reflection"
In the night I cannot sleep,
I rise and sit, plucking my resonant qín.
The thin curtains mirror the bright moon,
a clear breeze stirs my lapel.
A solitary swan cries beyond the wilds,
wheeling birds call in the northern woods.
I pace and wander, seeking what to see,
worried thoughts wound my lonely heart.
The Second
The Two Consorts stroll by the river,
care-free, soaring with the wind.
Jiāofǔ unwinds his jade belts,
with gentle grace and fragrant charm.
Their affection is tender and joyous,
across a thousand years never forgotten.
A city's fall beguiled Xià Cài,
beauty's countenance binds the innermost heart.
Stirred to passion, my worries rise,
xuāncǎo is planted beside the orchid chamber.
Ointments—for whom are they applied?
The raindrops resent the morning sun.
How is it that a friendship of gold and stone,
in a moment turns to parting and sorrow?
The Third
Under fine trees a pathway is formed,
peaches and plums flourish in the eastern garden.
Autumn winds scatter the beans,
from this moment comes their fall.
Flowers in bloom will fade and wither,
on the terrace sprout brambles and wolfberry.
I drive my horse and leave it behind,
departing, I stand at the foot of Xīshān.
Alone, I cannot secure myself,
how much less cling to wife and child!
Frost settles on the wild grass,
the year’s end too has come.
The Fourth
Heavenly horses come from the northwest,
but have always traveled the eastern road.
In Spring and Autumn there is no abiding place,
how can wealth and rank be kept for long?
Pure dew soaks the gaolán,
frost settles on the wild grasses.
In the morning, a charming youth,
by evening, aging and worn.
Unless one is Wáng Zǐjìn,
who can always remain fair and beautiful?
The Fifth
In my youthful years,
I was frivolous and loved pipe and song.
I journeyed west to Xiányáng,
with Zhào and Lǐ as my companions.
Amid amusements that knew no end,
the bright day suddenly slipped away.
I drove my horse and returned once more,
looking back toward Sānhé.
A hundred yi of gold is gone,
always there is want and need.
Northward I faced the Tàiháng road,
lost my way—what should I do!
The Sixth
In former times I heard of the Díng’s melons,
growing just outside Qīngmén.
Intertwined across fields and paths,
mother and child vines linked together.
Five colors shining in the morning sun,
fine guests gather from all directions.
Lamp oil burns itself away,
too much wealth brings harm and grief.
Plain garments may last a lifetime,
how can favor and riches be relied upon?
The Seventh
The summer heat—such is this season,
three tens of days are about to pass.
Fragrant trees suspend green leaves,
blue clouds wind far and long.
The four seasons change and alternate,
sun and moon shift and blur.
I wander atop an empty hall,
troubled, no one understands me.
I long to see lifelong happiness,
not to witness sorrow and parting.
The Eighth
Blazing, the western sun descends,
its last rays shine on my robe.
The turning wind sweeps the four walls,
cold birds seek each other in company.
Chóu-chóu birds still clasp their feathers,
the qióng-qióng also feel hunger.
How is it, those in the main road,
bow and break, forgetting where to return!
It is not for reputation or fame,
withered, my heart aches in sorrow.
Better to soar with sparrows and swallows,
than follow the lofty yellow crane.
The yellow crane roams the four seas,
mid-journey, where will it return?
The Ninth
Stepping out the Upper Eastern Gate,
looking north to Shǒuyáng peak.
Below are those who gather vetches,
above, the groves of fine trees.
Where is the good season now?
Frost clings to my coat.
Cold winds lash the hills,
dark clouds rise in heavy gloom.
Wild geese cry, flying southward,
tíjué birds sound a mournful note.
White forms drift with the shāng sound,
desolate, they wound my heart.
The Tenth
In the northern quarter are many strange dances,
above the Pú River, faint music drifts.
Frivolous, idle wanderers,
stoop and rise, floating or sinking.
Shortcuts are sought through narrow paths,
rushing toward wanton debauchery.
Where shall I see Wáng Zǐqiáo,
riding clouds through the Dèng Forest?
Only the art of longevity
can console my heart.
The Eleventh
The clear, vast waters of the Cháng Jiāng,
Above which grow groves of maple trees.
Tall orchids line the winding path,
Blue steeds swiftly flowing by.
A distant gaze moves the heart to sadness;
The spring air stirs my feelings.
In the Three Chǔs are many fine men,
Morning clouds drift into wildness and excess.
Vermilion flowers spread their fragrance,
Gāo Cài pursue one another in search.
Once, I wept for the yellow sparrow,
Who can hold back tears that fall?
Poem Twelve
Once, there was the child of splendor,
Ān Líng and Lóng Yáng.
Peach and plum blossoms, so young and tender,
Brilliant and radiant with shining light.
Charming and joyous as the springs of nine years,
Graceful like autumn frost.
With lingering glances, allure unfolds,
Words and laughter exhale sweet fragrance.
Hand in hand, sharing love equally;
Long ago, we shared quilt and robe.
May we be birds that fly together,
Soaring side by side on outstretched wings.
With paints and brush, a clear vow is set:
Never will we forget through all ages.
Poem Thirteen
Ascending high to overlook the fields,
Northward, gazing toward the green mountains.
Pines and cypress shade the ridges,
Flying birds call as they pass one another.
Moved with sighs and bitterness,
Long suffering the pain of resentment.
Lord Lǐ mourned at the eastern gate,
Sū Zǐ lamented the narrow Three Rivers.
Those who seek virtue, gain virtue themselves—
Why sigh and lament again?
Poem Fourteen
With autumn's coming, coolness rises,
Crickets chirp by the bed curtains.
Moved by things, my heart is filled with sorrow,
Quietly and softly, sadness enters my heart.
With so many words, who can I tell?
With elaborate speech, to whom will I confide?
A light breeze brushes my gauze sleeves,
The bright moon shines in pure radiance.
Morning roosters crow from tall trees,
I ready the carriage and prepare to return.
Poem Fifteen
In years past at fourteen or fifteen,
My aspirations cherished books and poetry.
Clad in rough cloth but harboring gems within,
Yán and Mǐn were my shared ideal.
Opening a window to overlook the fields,
Climbing high to long for those I think of.
Tombs cover the mountain ridges,
All generations become one in time.
A thousand autumns, ten thousand years from now,
Where does glorious fame ever go?
Thus, I understand the wisdom of Xiàn Ménzǐ,
Lamenting and sighing, I laugh at myself.
Poem Sixteen
Pacing atop the pond of wild grass,
I turn and gaze toward Dà Liáng.
Green waters raise their mighty waves,
Wastelands sprawl vast and endless.
Beasts run and dart, crossing each other;
Birds fly, accompanying one another.
At this time, the fires of late summer rage,
Sun and moon gaze at each other.
A north wind sharpens the bitter cold,
Yin vapors fall as light frost.
Traveling afar, I have no companion,
Lowering and raising my head, I feel sorrow.
Petty men count their achievements,
Noble men uphold constancy.
How could I care if I end in decline—
I chant these lines to set forth my thoughts.
Poem Seventeen
Alone, I sit atop an empty hall—
Who is there to share my joy?
Out the door lies the endless road,
Horse-drawn carriages are seen no more.
Climbing high, I look over the Nine Provinces,
Stretching far into the vast wilderness.
A lone bird flies northwest,
Separated beasts head southeast.
At dusk, I yearn for kin and friends,
I speak my feelings to express myself.
Poem Eighteen
The suspended carriage is in the southwest,
Xī Hé is about to descend.
Radiant light shines on the Four Seas,
In a flash, evening darkness arrives.
In the morning, it is the brilliance of Xiánchí,
Méng Sì bathes in this glory.
How could those trapped or successful know—
Once dead, there is no rebirth.
Looking at the peach and plum blossoms,
Who can long remain bright and shining?
Where is the noble man now?
With sighs, we remain apart,
Gazing up at the pines on Jǐngshān,
They may comfort my heart.
Poem Nineteen
In the west there is a fair beauty,
Bright as the shining sun.
She wears delicate gauze robes,
At her waist, double huáng ornaments.
Refined features radiate beauty,
Riding the wind, sending forth gentle fragrance.
Climbing high to search for her longing,
She lifts her sleeve to face the morning sun.
Her countenance rests amid the floating clouds,
She waves her sleeves, soaring into the void.
Drifting, uncertain, between illusion and reality,
She glances sideways, near me.
Joy and gladness, yet we have not met;
Speaking thus, I am moved to sorrow.
Poem Twenty
Yáng Zhū wept at the crossroads,
Mòzǐ mourned for the dyed silk.
Bowing and yielding, long have we parted,
Drifting along, it is hard to agree on a time.
How could it be only the love of swallows and doves?
Life and death truly coexist.
Desolation is what men mourn,
Disaster and strife cannot be refused.
The Lady of Zhào charmed Zhōng Shān,
But her humility drew even greater abuse.
Alas, those on the road to greatness,
How can they maintain themselves?
Poem Twenty-One
Deep in my heart, I treasure every moment,
The sun of Xī Yáng is about to set.
Waving my sleeve and grasping my long sword,
I look up and watch the journey of floating clouds.
Between the clouds is a mysterious crane,
Lofty is its will, its cry sorrowful.
With one flight, it soars to the blue heavens,
Through the ages, it will not cry again.
How can it play with quails and sparrows,
Flitting endlessly in the courtyard?
Poem Twenty-Two
The descendant of Xià rides a cloud carriage,
Kuāfù becomes the forest of Dèng.
Existence and nonexistence follow change,
Sun and moon rise and fall.
The phoenix sings in discordant tones,
Líng Lún brings forth its music.
The prince loves pipes and flutes,
Generation after generation seeks each other.
Who says they cannot be seen?
The green bird reveals my feelings.
Poem Twenty-Three
To the southeast stands Shè Shān,
Where the Fén River rises to its sunny side.
Six dragons draw the vapor carriage,
Canopy of clouds brushes heaven’s web.
There are four or five immortals,
Roaming at ease in Yàn Lán’s chambers.
Sleeping peacefully in pure harmony,
Their breath becomes dew and frost.
They bathe in the cinnabar pool,
Shining with the light of the sun and moon.
Why remain at the Lingtái of tranquility?
Roam wide and soar high away.
Poem Twenty-Four
Endless sorrow knots my ambitions,
Apprehension always startles me as if in fear.
Carefree wandering can never last,
The vermilion sun suddenly leans to the west.
Crickets sing by the door and window,
Cicadas cry from within the courtyard.
Our hearts are not at peace together—
Who can say they truly know my feelings?
I wish to be a bird amid the clouds,
Crying in sorrow for a thousand li.
The Three Divine Herbs lengthen the Isles of Yíngzhōu,
Traveling far may bring long life.
Poem Twenty-Five
Drawing the sword before white blades,
how could we inflict wounds upon one another?
I only fear the words of talented men,
who speak of me by the Sanjiāng rivers.
Flying springs stream down Yùshān,
suspended carriages roost at Fúsāng.
Sun and moon traverse a thousand li,
pure winds raise subtle frosts.
The path to power has prosperity and decline,
how could lamenting last forever?
Number Twenty-Six
At dawn I climb Hóngpō’s summit,
day and night gazing toward Xīshān.
Thorns and brambles cover the plains,
flocks of birds fly in fluttering crowds.
Luán and yī pause to perch and rest,
life has its own nature.
Who can approach Jiànmù,
she who is bright as the shègān flower?
I do not see the kudzu in the forest,
its creeping vines link in embrace.
Number Twenty-Seven
Zhōu and Zhèng ties span the land,
the streets meet at Sānhé.
A charming young woman of the city,
shining with what splendid blossoms.
Dark hair frames rosy cheeks,
her sidelong glance shines with brilliance.
A glimpse topples the city’s will,
her passing gaze makes others boast.
I wish to roam for three springs,
but morning sun is gone in a trice.
Fame and decline come in a moment,
how shall we endure farewells?
Number Twenty-Eight
Were flowers to blaze across the four seas,
their brightness would shade Yíngzhōu beyond Fúsāng.
Sun and moon travel the road of heaven,
light and dark do not oppose each other.
Severe clarity keeps its constant,
gain and loss—what is there to pursue?
Could I act like the children along the road,
hand in hand frolicking together?
Yin and yang have transformations,
who can say what sinks will not float again?
The red tortoise leaps in flying springs,
by night it flies over Wúzhōu.
Raising and bowing move Heaven and Earth,
again I caress the four flowing seas.
Fame and profit bind us all,
slow and swift yoked to the same shaft.
How much better to leave ear and eye behind,
ascend afar and escape gloomy sorrow.
Number Twenty-Nine
Once I traveled to Dàliáng,
climbing to the summit of Huánghuā.
Gònggōng dwells in the dark,
a tall platform reaching the blue heavens.
Vast and remote, wild and desolate,
sorrowfully I recall whom I love.
Who is it I cherish?
Bright discernment illumines beauty.
Yìnglóng sinks beneath Jìzhōu,
the enchanting girl cannot sleep.
Indulging arrogance atop worldly ways,
how could one say she’ll endure eternal years!
Number Thirty
Driving my carriage I leave the gate,
intending for a far journey.
Where should this journey go?
Turning my back on boast and fame.
Boasted fame is not my own,
only may I fulfill my true heart.
A single curtain shields the bright sun,
high balconies muffle faint sounds.
Slander and deceit estrange friends,
floating clouds make day grow dark.
Lovely as a lady’s garments,
a mere glance can topple cities.
Peace comes with a moment,
luxuriant bloom does not last twice.
Morning swiftly becomes dusk,
I see not the face I cherish.
Yellow birds fly southeast,
send my words to thank my friends.
Number Thirty-One
With reins in hand I depart Wèidū,
looking south toward Chuītái.
Flutes and pipes echo lingering notes,
where is King Liáng now?
Soldiers feed on chaff and husks,
the worthy dwell among weeds.
Song and dance are not yet ended,
Qín troops arrive once more.
Ave-lined woods are not mine,
the vermilion palace gathers dust.
The army fell beneath Huáyáng,
the body at last becomes dust and ashes.
Number Thirty-Two
The rising sun blooms but once,
the white day suddenly enters dark west.
To leave here is but a glance,
how akin to nine autumns.
Life is like dust or dew,
the way of heaven stretches distant and vast.
Qíjǐng ascended the tumulus,
tears streaming in profusion.
Kǒngshèng gazed upon the long river,
sorrowing for fleeting time.
The gone, I cannot reach;
the coming I cannot keep.
Let me ascend Tàihuà Mountain,
joining Sōngzǐ above.
The fisherman understands worldly troubles,
riding the current on a light boat.
Number Thirty-Three
One day follows one evening,
one night follows one dawn.
Complexion alters from the usual,
spirit wanes away of itself.
Within the breast is boiling turmoil,
transformation ever calls in turn.
Of all affairs there is no end,
wise plans prove bitterly unkind.
I only fear in a brief instant,
my spirit will be swept by the wind.
Lifelong I tread on thin ice,
who knows the anxiety in my heart!
Number Thirty-Four
One day follows one dawn,
one dusk follows one morning.
Features grow unlike before,
spirit drifts and is lost.
Before the beaker much sorrow arises,
I think on those I knew before.
Facing wine I cannot speak,
my heart is full of grief and bitterness.
Wishing to till the eastern bank,
but who will join me in keeping true?
Sorrow dwells in the moment,
noble conduct wounds a humble self.
Bent or straight, what does it matter?
Dragons and serpents are my neighbors.
Number Thirty-Five
Worldly affairs are ever tangled,
human ways suffer for lack of respite.
Vigor of youth passes with time,
morning dew awaits the sun.
I wish to seize Xīhé’s reins,
that the white sun not shift in its light.
Heaven’s stairs and paths break off,
the Silver River is far without a bridge.
Washing my hair at the shore of Yánggǔ,
roaming far by Kūnyuè’s side.
Climbing those cliffs of immortals,
picking these sweet autumn orchids.
What use to strive for worldly roads?
In Tàijí one may freely soar.
Number Thirty-Six
Who says all affairs are difficult?
Unfettered, one may end their days.
On the hall, shaded by flowering trees,
I muse on the unseen.
Wandering, I think of dear friends,
in a moment suddenly reaching the underworld.
I send word by birds flying east,
may they comfort my feelings.
Number Thirty-Seven
The auspicious time is in this hour,
light rain sprinkles the dust.
By the wayside, longing for those I miss,
day and night they do not come.
Feelings surge within the heart,
its ripples cannot be stilled.
Wiping tears I nurse my grief,
my bitterness—who can I tell?
Number Thirty-Eight
Fiery radiance stretches ten thousand lǐ,
the broad river surges with swift rapids.
A curved bow hangs on Fúsāng,
a long sword leans beyond the heavens.
Tàishān serves as a whetstone,
the Huánghé as a sash around the waist.
Looking at Zhuāng Zhōu-zǐ,
how can one rely on fortune and decay?
To throw away one’s body, abandoned in the wilderness,
and let crows and kites become harm—
how could this compare to the heroic worthies,
whose fame and achievement become great from here?
The Thirty-Ninth
How resolute the brave man is!
His ambition is to awe the Eight Wastes.
He drives his chariot out on distant campaigns,
obeying his orders, forgetting himself in thought.
A fine bow holds a crow-feathered arrow,
a bright armor shines with exquisite light.
Facing hardship, he does not care for life;
dead, his soul soars flying.
Is he one who cherishes his whole body?
He devotes himself, contending on the battlefield.
Loyalty brings honor for generations,
righteousness makes a fair name illustrious.
His reputation endures after,
for integrity and resolve ever remain.
The Fortieth
Chaos begets the Two Principles,
Four Symbols revolve the armillary sphere.
The bright sun diffuses fiery essence,
the pale moon hangs with radiant light.
The movement of time circles clearly,
alas! human life is frail indeed!
Drifting away as dust on the wind,
vanishing suddenly like auspicious clouds dried by the sun.
Cultivating long life suits my wish,
but glory and favor are not my own power.
Ān Qī treads the heavenly path,
Sōngzǐ departs from the mundane world.
How could I gain wings to soar sky-high,
floating to ascend the verge of clouds?
Alas, the resolve of Ní Fù!
Why does he dwell among the Jiǔ Yí?
The Forty-First
Heaven’s net covers the open fields,
six wings folded, unable to unfurl.
A traveler tossed on the waves,
drifting aimlessly like a floating duck.
Life and death have no fixed measure;
each dawn and dusk brings the unexpected.
The immortals have halted their pursuit of longevity,
nurturing purpose in pure emptiness.
Floating high amid clouds and sun,
far from the ways of the world.
Fame is not my treasure,
how can sounds and sights suffice for joy?
Seeking herbs, there is no return,
the immortal’s resolve does not match my own.
Forced thus, how confusing it is,
making me hesitate long.
The Forty-Second
The king’s enterprise must have worthy aides,
to accomplish deeds, he awaits heroes.
Yuán Kǎi’s virtue is splendid,
many worthies praise him in song.
Yin and Yang at times are at odds,
sun and moon do not always blend in harmony.
Heavenly times have fortune or misfortune,
human affairs are full or empty, waxing and waning.
Yuán Qǐ withdrew to the southern peak,
Bóyáng hid among the Western Róng.
To protect oneself, keep true to the Way,
as for fame and honor, what value are they?
Who among people does not begin well?
Few can perfect the end.
Fortunate indeed, the worthies of old,
whose pure reputation endures for ten thousand ages!
The Forty-Third
Geese and swans soar together in flight,
flying, flying to distant wastelands.
Paired wings face the long wind,
in an instant, they are ten thousand lǐ away.
In the morning, they eat jade-like berries,
at night, they rest on crimson mountain slopes.
Aloft among the blue clouds,
what net or snare could control them?
How could they mix with villagers,
joining hands to swear shallow oaths?
The Forty-Fourth
All beings differ from start to end;
long or short, each finds its own path.
Jadestone bamboo grows on lofty mountains,
magic mushrooms shine in vermilion halls.
Bright shine the blossoms of peach and plum,
forming paths, yet soon withered and harmed.
How dare one covet a thousand arts?
In the third spring only a slight light appears.
If not a tree that stands against the wind,
how could it ever stay unbowed and unchanging?
The Forty-Fifth
Hidden orchids cannot be worn,
for whom does the vermilion grass shine?
Tall bamboo conceals itself in shady hills,
shègān grows by the ramparts of Zēngchéng.
Grape vines trail in distant valleys,
endless gourds and melons grow and wind.
At greatest joy, spirit disperses,
deep sorrow wounds the soul.
Surely one learns anxiety is fruitless;
how much better to return to the Grand Purity!
The Forty-Sixth
The false dove flies among mulberry and elm,
sea birds soar across heaven and earth.
Surely they know vastness,
but their wings are not the same.
How can the Pole Star be reached in flight?
It is better to roost on tree branches.
They alight among mugwort and wormwood below,
above, they play on garden fences.
Thus are they content with themselves,
why use you as companions in pursuit?
The Forty-Seventh
Where is the span of life and time?
Sorrow and grief make tears wet the robe.
High birds soar among mountain ridges,
swallows and sparrows nest in low forests.
Blue clouds shroud the forecourt,
the white zither grieves my heart.
In lofty hills cranes cry out,
how could I seek them there?
The Forty-Eighth
The calling dove plays among courtyard trees,
Jiao Míng rides drifting clouds.
Where can I see the lone flying bird,
flitting with none in matching flock?
Life and death obey the natural order,
dispersing and vanishing in confusion.
The Forty-Ninth
I stroll beside the crossroads,
saddened, longing for what I think of.
It is not for today’s meeting,
yet suddenly, it truly seems so.
Within the marsh, lofty pines grow,
whose lifespan can never be determined.
The high-flying bird brushes the sky,
together soaring and playing amidst the clouds.
How could there be a lone traveler,
weeping for bygone times?
The Fiftieth
Pure dew becomes congealed frost,
splendid herbs turn to weeds.
Who says a gentleman is virtuous—
how can discernment and wisdom be relied upon?
Ride the clouds, summon Sōng Qiáo,
call and sigh—so may it last forever!
The Fifty-First
The loyal heart loses favor and grace,
great virtue loses its due.
How can good words always last?
Kindness is not easily given.
Do you not see the south-flying swallow,
its wings just out of alignment?
Gāo Zǐ laments in new poetry,
Sān Lú grieves separation.
Why does Hun Dùn ever change,
and in a twinkling, body and form collapse?
The Fifty-Second
Ten suns rise from Yánggǔ,
holding reins, they gallop ten thousand lǐ.
Traversing the skies, they shine on the Four Seas,
in an instant, they hide in mist and haze.
Who says blazing sunlight endures?
Journeying afar, when should it wait?
That which departs cannot become immortal,
it too leaves jīng trees and qǐ.
A thousand years is but a morning,
a single meal suffices for oneself.
Between right and wrong, gain and loss,
how can one’s judgment be perfect?
When calculating gain, skill reaches its end,
and sorrow can suddenly be stilled.
The Fifty-Third
Nature has its established principles,
the way of life and death is ever-changing.
A thousand ingenious devices and ideas arise,
but the essential foundation does not alter.
Why does Kuā Pízi [夸毗子] boast,
making a show and harboring arrogance in his heart?
He rides in a carriage and drives fine horses,
leaning idly on tables and feasting on delicacies.
He wears garments of delicate thin silk,
and builds secluded chambers in deep pavilions.
He does not see the glory of the setting sun,
as he flutters by the wayside.
Number Fifty-Four
He boasts and vents his exasperation,
his indolence brings vexation to his heart.
To the northwest, he climbs Bù Zhōu [不周],
to the southeast, gazes toward Dèng Lín [鄧林].
The wide wilds span the nine provinces,
lofty mountains tower with high peaks.
A single meal crosses ten thousand ages,
a thousand years, floating and sinking again.
Who says jade and stone are the same?
Tears fall unrestrained.
Number Fifty-Five
People speak of wishing to prolong life,
but if you prolong it, where would you go with it?
The yellow swan calls to Zǐ Ān [子安],
but a thousand autumns are still too far to expect.
Alone, I sit in the mountain cave,
sorrowful for the one on my mind.
How admirable was Prince Wáng Zǐ [王子]!
How elegant as we supported one another.
Joy and happiness were as of this very moment,
the reckoning was but for an instant.
Put aside thoughts of tomorrow,
for every day brings fresh deceits.
Number Fifty-Six
Nobility and lowliness lie in Heaven’s decree,
success and failure have their appointed times.
Coy and scheming flatterers,
pursue profit and come to deceive me.
Lonely, I think of losing Huì Shī [惠施],
but it is only for the sake of slanderous men’s mockery.
The wagtail sings among the clouds,
rising and flying with no certain aim.
Who knows the fickleness of men?
In a single day, they cannot be depended upon.
Number Fifty-Seven
A fierce wind shakes the four wilds,
whirling clouds shade the corner of the hall.
For whom is the bed’s canopy arranged?
For whom does the staff support?
Though I am not a wise gentleman,
am I as blind as the mulberry and elm?
There exist in this world such deaf and blind men,
adrift, what can be done?
Lightly, I drift with the wind,
leisurely, I leave my old home.
I take my leave beneath the Jade Mountain [玉山],
abandoning both praise and slander.
Number Fifty-Eight
A high hat brushes the floating clouds,
a long sword thrusts beyond the heavens.
What need to trouble over trifles?
Lofty ambitions span an age.
If it were not you who guided me,
how could I wander freely at the world’s edge?
I glance back, bidding farewell to the Xī Wángmǔ [西王母],
for I shall depart from here.
Would I, then, dwell with men of humble doors,
plucking the zither and chanting their oaths?
Number Fifty-Nine
Upon the riverbank dwells an old man,
weaving sedge and casting away bright pearls.
He is content with eating wild herbs and beans,
delighted in a hut of mugwort and wormwood.
How could he imitate those who strive for show,
driving fine horses and light carriages?
Born beside crossroads in the morning,
by dusk he is buried on the byways.
Merriment does not endure until dusk,
sighing with head bowed and raised.
Witnessing these two or three examples,
resentment is thereby eased.
Number Sixty
The scholar understands the Six Arts,
sets his resolve unyielding.
Violating ritual, he is unmoved,
unlawful speech he will not utter.
If thirsty, he drinks from clear streams,
when hungry, eats only a single basket of food.
At the year’s end he cannot perform rites,
his clothes are always worn and cold.
Slippers on his feet, he sings the “South Wind,”
wearing a coarse robe, he laughs at splendid carriages.
He keeps faith with the Way and guards books of poetry,
justice will not accept even a single meal.
With fierce words of praise and blame,
Lǎo Zǐ [老氏] can only heave a long sigh!
Number Sixty-One
In youth, he learned fencing,
mastering skill beyond Qū Chéng [曲城].
With heroic spirit cleaving clouds and rainbows,
he surpasses the age and utters strange sounds.
Wielding his sword he faces the desert,
watering his horse in the nine wilds.
How flutter the banners and pennants,
while only the sound of drums and bells is heard.
Campaigns bring sorrow to men,
intense vigor has its griefs.
I recall my ordinary days,
regret and repentance are born from this.
Number Sixty-Two
In the calm of day, I straighten my robe and cap,
hoping to receive guests and visitors.
But who are these guests?
Suddenly they are gone like blowing dust.
Their robes are cloud-tinted,
their speech penetrates spirit and soul.
But in a moment, all have turned and left;
when again shall I meet such men?
Number Sixty-Three
Too much care scatters the will,
loneliness makes the heart grieve.
I soar to gaze on ponds and marshes,
draw my sword and board a light boat.
I only wish for long leisure,
and in future years to come again and wander.
Number Sixty-Four
At dawn I depart by the Upper Eastern Gate,
gazing far toward Shǒu Yáng [首陽].
Thick pine and cypress stand in dense array,
yellow orioles together at play.
I wander at ease among the winding paths,
loitering, uncertain where to go.
I think of my ordinary days,
and brooding, recall the lovely courtesan.
Number Sixty-Five
Prince Wáng Zǐ [王子] at fifteen years
wandered at the banks of Yī-Luò [伊洛].
His rosy cheeks were as spring flowers,
persuasive and wise with an upright heart.
Where could one find Fú Qiū Gōng [浮丘公]?
With raised hand, he bids farewell to people of the world.
Restless, easy to become lost in thought,
drifting and forsaking his own body.
He flies and calls as he soars,
beating his wings in sorrow.
Number Sixty-Six
The gates of the fortress cannot be passed,
how could one float on the sea?
In bright dawn I do not see my friend,
suddenly enveloped in darkness, without a protector.
Bearing a melon, I think longingly of Dōng Líng [東陵];
the yellow sparrow is truly left in shame.
Disfavor comes in a moment,
so I gird my sword and ascend Wú Qiū [吾丘].
I mourn for the master of the mulberry woods,
tears streaming down my face.
Borrowing a steed to travel between Qiān and Wèi [汧渭],
with horse and saddle I go journey afar.
Number Sixty-Seven
Hóng Shēng [洪生] accords with the proper order,
his attire is always fitting.
Superior and inferior are assigned their rank,
affairs and objects are orderly and regulated.
He composes his appearance and countenance,
bowing low with tablet in hand.
On the hall is placed sacrificial wine,
within the house, stores of grain and rice.
Outwardly, he maintains solemn discourse,
indoors, he stifles all fragrance.
Speaking openly from his heart,
he again expounds upon the Way of righteousness.
With subtlety, he conducts himself according to ceremony,
yet his manner fills me with sorrow.
Number Sixty-Eight
Northward, I approach the Qiánmèi Stream,
traveling westward to roam at Shàorèn.
From afar, I gaze toward Tiānjīn,
my heart filled with pleasure and contentment.
The intricate and resplendent gate of life and death—
once I visit, I will not seek it again.
If perchance I encounter the morning wind bird,
I will fly and ride forth out of the southern woods.
Vast and boundless amid the radiance of jade,
I drift on, yielding to wanton indulgence.
I rest peacefully at Qīngdū Palace,
who, in transcending the world, could restrain me?
Poem Sixty-Nine
People know how to form alliances,
but true friendship is especially hard to find.
On perilous roads there is much suspicion and doubt,
and a bright pearl is not easily procured.
Some seek feast at the grandest tables,
I only wish for a simple meal.
Gain and loss breed resentment and malice,
again and again—what more can be said?
Poem Seventy
Where there is sorrow, there is feeling,
where there is no sorrow, there is also no thought.
If one is not ensnared by net and trap,
why journey ten thousand miles from home?
Soaring winds brush the high clouds,
fortunate clouds invite the chosen.
With ashes of the heart entrusted to a withered dwelling,
why gaze upon mortal forms?
From the first, forgetting oneself is difficult;
who can know how one silently forsakes oneself?
Poem Seventy-One
The hibiscus flourishes on the mound of graves,
shining brightly with splendid colors.
The sun sets within the forest,
gracefully it falls to the wayside.
Crickets sing at the window and door,
cicadas chirp within the brambles and thorns.
Mayflies sport for but three mornings,
plucking and tending their slender wings.
For whom is this fine clothing worn?
Bowing and raising, one wipes it oneself.
How long is the span of life?
With fervor, let each strive on.
Poem Seventy-Two
Down the long road, the carriage speeds forth;
across the broad river, a light boat ferries along.
Is life truly a matter of nature?
The path to power is not without cause.
Lofty reputation confounds the will,
greed for riches troubles the heart.
Intimacy conceals suspicion,
even kin may become one’s foe.
Still hoping to destroy pearls and jade—
such could be used to ascend and roam.
Poem Seventy-Three
Among lateral strategists is a remarkable man,
Huángjùn harnessed to his carriage.
In the morning, he rises in the wilds of Yíngzhōu,
by night, rests at Míngguāng Palace.
Again he surveys the lands beyond the four seas,
with plumage and wings, he soars on his own.
Leaving aside worldly matters,
how could they ever vex my innermost being?
Once gone, it is forevermore a parting,
for a thousand years, gazing at each other from afar.
Poem Seventy-Four
Ah, the men of ancient times—
serene and content, their will at peace in poverty.
As the later era’s teachings declined,
people raced, beset by turmoil and dust.
Was Níngzǐ not of their kind?
Who would still raise a song and follow?
The restless are not my companions,
the wandering not of my kin.
Ah, the affairs of honor and disgrace—
depart and savor the true Way!
The true Way is assuredly delightful,
purity preserves the spirit within.
Cháoyóu held up his lofty virtue,
and from hence journeyed to the river's edge.
Poem Seventy-Five
East of Liáng there is fragrant grass,
blossoming time and again in a single morning.
Its appearance is radiant, posture exquisite,
its luster dazzling, overturning the whole city.
Is it only for the wise and worthy?
Allure and flattery breed toadies.
Frivolity lasts but a moment,
how can one know a hundred generations' renown?
At the lane’s end stands a graceful woman,
only fearing the sun and moon will fall.
Where can we see the spirit tree?
Vast and remote, it has no formed presence.
Poem Seventy-Six
How can one learn to drive the autumn chariot?
Dōngyě lingers by the deserted roadside.
The line sinks deep, the fish keeping to the abyss;
the snare is set, the bird soars high above.
Drifting, one boards a light boat,
floating idly, with nothing in sight to seek.
Who benefits from flattery and boasting?
By river and lake, all is forgotten and cast away.
The beautiful face is hard to preserve,
but to keep a refined appearance is my constant.
In these years at Sōng and Qiáo,
shadows and illusions are truly without end.
Poem Seventy-Seven
Ah, in a flash we journey until old age;
bowed and burdened by constant worries.
Gazing at the river, I envy its great waves:
our origins are the same but our courses diverge.
What worth is a century's life?
Only pain from grudges and enmity.
Who are these foes and rivals?
Ears and eyes turn away in mutual shame.
Sounds and colors are like the lands of Hú and Yuè,
human feelings force themselves to rigidity.
I summon that adept of profound understanding,
let us leave and return to the land of yearning journeys.
Poem Seventy-Eight
Of old there lived an immortal man,
dwelling amid the slopes of Shè Mountain.
He rode clouds and drove flying dragons,
breathing and exhaling amidst Qiónghuá.
One could hear of him but not see him,
gallant and moved, I sigh in lament.
Feeling pained, not being of his kind,
sorrows and griefs come to press upon me.
To learn below and ascend above—
suddenly, what should I do?
Poem Seventy-Nine
Within the forest is a wondrous bird,
declaring itself to be the fènghuáng.
At dawn it drinks from the pure spring,
by dusk, it nests on the mountain ridge.
It sings high and clear across the nine provinces,
raising its neck to gaze across the eight wilds.
Just as it meets the merchant wind,
its feathers and wings break and hide away.
Once departed to the west of Kūnlún,
when again will it return in flight?
I only regret dwelling out of place,
sorrow and regret wound my heart.
Poem Eighty
I step outside and look for the lovely one,
but is the lovely one truly here?
From the Three Mountains, Sōng and Qiáo beckon,
who across ten thousand generations can make a pact?
Life and death possess their length and shortness,
how can one know greatness by resolve alone?
Alas, the morning sun hastens to its end;
as I go on and on, where am I to head?
I see not the late autumn grass,
withered and broken in these times.
Poem Eighty-One
There once were immortals,
Xiànmén and Sōngqiáo among them.
Breathing and practicing among the Nine Suns,
they soared high into the swirling clouds.
Human life finds joy in endurance;
a hundred years seem but distant talk.
The sun falls into the valley’s edge,
one night passes, it does not dawn again.
How unlike the remnants of worldly things,
ascending to brilliance, drifting free with the wind.
Poem Eighty-Two
That which glimmers before the tomb—
the hibiscus dazzles with vermilion blossoms.
Its beauty ends before the morning is through,
in a whirlwind its flowers vanish.
How much better the grass of the western hills,
bamboo gems and red rice.
Their shade hangs over Zēngchéng,
remaining radiance shines across the nine valleys.
Would that there were a youth,
alas, with the days long, lament is hard to bear.
Two Songs
“Song of the Woodcutter”
The sun sets beyond the western limits of Bùzhōu,
the moon rises from within the scarlet depths.
The pure essence of yang is obscured from sight,
and the cold light of yin takes its place in dominance.
Lofty and upright for but a moment,
soon it fades away, then rises anew.
Clouds and mists gather and part,
coming and going like a rushing wind.
Wealth and honor pass in a glance up or down,
poverty and lowliness need not last forever.
Liú Hóu rose from fugitive ranks,
his might and power struck awe in wild wastes.
Shào Píng was granted the fief of Dōnglíng,
yet one morning he became a commoner.
Branches and leaves rely on the roots for support,
life and death together share prosperity and decline.
Those who attain success ascend by destiny,
those who lose power fall with the times.
Cold and heat follow one after another,
transformations ever push each other onward.
Calamity and fortune have no constant master,
so why worry if you lack a home?
Pushing forward by this principle,
why bewail gathering firewood again?
“Song of the Great Teacher”
Heaven and earth dissolve, the six directions open wide,
stars fall, and sun and moon topple down;
if I soar aloft, what longing would I bear!
“Rhapsody on Dōngpíng”
The Nine Provinces have their shapes of square and round,
the nine wilds have their own lay of the land,
each region with height and depth,
each thing has its own measure:
Open, it is accessible;
Blocked, it is closed;
Let it flow, it moves on;
Dam it, and it stops;
Raise it, and hills are formed;
Lower it, it becomes marsh and lake;
winding and spreading wide,
encircled by great ravines.
When nations and cities are divided,
and visible things are arrayed,
the four seasons present their images,
yīn and yáng play forth their energies,
passing through and returning,
possessing form and virtue,
clouds rise, thunder rumbles,
now a shout, now a hush;
some attain security thus,
yet others are perplexed thereby.
If you look upon corners left vacant,
desolate and wild tracts,
spaces of unbounded emptiness,
settlements at the ends of the wilds;
strange and marvelous, twisted and bizarre,
they defy exhaustible description.
Thus are there those who roam everywhere,
cultivating noble reserve,
braving shocking winds,
treading floating clouds,
the pure and the foul both flowing past,
fortune and misfortune answering each other.
Therefore Líng Lún wandered with the phoenix on Mount Kūnlún's southern slopes,
Zōu Zǐ breathed warmth in the shade of Shǔgǔ,
Bó Gāo ascended and descended on Shàngjì's heights,
Xiàn Mén roamed freely atop the peaks of the Three Mountains;
above they soared in the Mystic Park,
below wandered through the forests of Dèng.
Phoenixes sang on their own,
luan birds danced without prompting,
fine grains flourished in abundance,
though none of it was my millet or rice.
But in low, constricted places, there are the plains of unruly acts,
the haunts of deer and pigs,
not a land of refined purity and splendor,
but a place of filth and shame.
To the west stands the crag of Āzhēn,
connected at the sides to Qīpú,
in the mulberry groves above the Pǔ River,
the haunts of reckless dissipation.
The lands of the Three Jìn run free and wild,
Zhèng and Wèi are rife with turmoil,
the bold and clever overbear their followers,
while the followers idle in residence.
Thus the strong and violent impose at doors and windows,
resentment and malice flare at the corners of beds,
evils arise from village feasts,
there is no need to wait long for trouble to appear.
Its soil is truly central,
where the Liú royal clan gathers.
High and perilous looks down on the city,
deep rivers circle its dwellings.
Shū clan marriages and kinships,
truly reside at its edge,
turning their back to danger, facing the water,
much foulness and much secrecy.
Thus their villages and towns,
none may speak against,
with deadened feelings and warped plans,
seeking only to increase their wealth.
Their farmlands are wild and desolate,
trees and crops grown out of season,
fields left untilled,
brambles left unchecked,
stagnant ponds and wasted pools,
overflowing and wild without control.
East it faces the Three Qí,
west it adjoins Zōu and Lǔ,
long roads stretch a thousand miles,
all taken as trade routes;
laborers work at leisure as their rule,
soldiery is used as support,
the arrogant serve the petty townships,
and here they make their home.
Rivers and marshes offer shortcuts,
passing Dòngtíng, Jīng, and Chǔ,
customs from ages past pass through,
this is both their way and abode.
Through this they inherit local ways,
what is followed is what is seen,
not the law of the barbarians,
but guidance leading to ruin.
Therefore their songs and harmonies boast of power,
turning their back to principle and seeking craftiness,
drifting with desires, chasing profit,
moved by fear, ever prone to fault.
Their dwellings are cramped, dark, blocked off,
deep and secluded without clarity,
leaning on tombs for support,
twined with winding rooms;
thus living there dulls the heart,
speaking of it grieves the mind,
uneasy and troubled, hard to change,
unable to awaken the mind’s longing.
Outside, the muddy Huáng Hé circles its pools,
the clear Jì River cleanses its border.
To the north lie continuous hills,
steep and rugged,
mountain ridges tall and lofty,
clouds and lightning mingling together,
long winds sweep fiercely,
vast plains stretch in desolation.
To the south, the floating Wèn is limpid and clear,
wash from floods forms pools,
deep forests and lush trees,
thick and dense, uneven in growth,
flocks of birds soar in the sky,
herds of beasts run together.
Though the common people are not good,
their mountains and marshes stretch far and wide.
The wise men of old cared little for status,
delighting in government and ritual as fitting acts.
Cherished by the mystics,
they delight in tranquil obscurity, knowing nothing.
Alas, the scattered feelings of the villages and alleys,
rise on the returning wind to be voiced aloud.
Gazing at the wild thickets, so weedy and foul,
looking back at Dōngshān, so lush and green.
Clinging to the old words of Qiū and Lǐ,
I compose new verses to comfort my feelings.
Truly, the harsh frost has not yet spread,
how could the cinnabar trees flourish again?
“The Northern Gate” is bitter with deep sorrow,
“Lesser Biàn” laments unrequited devotion.
Ōu Duān yī once longed for humaneness,
how such simple honesty could not be displayed;
The model of birds stirred his will,
how much less could an unworthy man respond.
Now, with heart oppressed and thoughts wandering afar,
I long to return, riding on the whirling gale.
Qīn Pī roams atop the hills’ crests,
leading this host to soar in contest.
Things evolve and spirits find joy,
so how could one fail to pursue a far-off vision?
I ride a pine-wood boat to cross treacherous paths,
though without mooring, I am self-restrained.
I drive a huáliú on a narrow road,
yet glance back at the lame donkey who cannot keep up.
Relying on a zhāngfǔ hat, I journey to Yuè,
and upon seeing the glow of the rhinoceros, I enter before others;
draped in embroidered silks, I trade with the Rong,
knowing well that fur robes must always be adopted.
Embracing the unspoiled virtue of balance and harmony,
who in this land is fit to gather together?
Desiring to speak of returning to fine customs,
I invite the Prince to roam together.
Rinsing my mouth with the nectar of jade, nourishing and pleasing,
I drink pure water from a clear stream.
Then I set my heart to emptiness and cease only afterward,
so what reason have I to harbor any sorrow or worry?
Again it is said:
I praise the pure clarity of a fortunate year,
rejoicing in the spring sunshine that ushers in summer.
Entrusting my thoughts to the gale as my vehicle,
I harness the form and body to make a chariot.
Following the idle paths and driving far ahead,
I ask the boughed winds about my confusion and perplexity.
Dark clouds rise and encircle all around,
cold rains fall down and descend.
Suddenly awakened and I lose my course,
I tread the empty void and thus journey onward.
A whirlwind is shrouded at Héxū,
the Xiánchí reflects on Zēngchéng.
Delighting in the sparkling brilliance of dawn’s radiance,
enjoying the blazing essence of the sun.
Measuring the drifting boat amid anxious reflection,
I linger carefree upon the pure vast sea.
Carefully attending to the truthful instructions of the dark mystery,
I imagine the sage appearing with form.
Though the embroidery is dazzling, I see not its chaos,
my thoughts travel further as I measure what is near;
together we pivot our chariots along ditches and canals,
as if the empty mulberry grove could be immediately reached.
Words spill forth without end,
my heart is boundless and never rests.
I collect unhurried admonitions for self-reflection,
sighing at the difficulty of fathoming the multitude of teachings.
My spirit travels far to find repose,
fearing the twin rings at my side.
I consult with birds who do not flock together,
and mourn for the endless vastness.
All value how easily wild herbs can be cultivated,
grasping the mutual praise of those near at hand.
Afraid of following the wind and departing forever,
I entrust myself to Zhuān Xū at the distant corner.
Though the instruments qín and sè remain intact,
how could their harmonious melodies be played once more?
Longing to roam in search of the extraordinary,
how can those rising aloft be surpassed?
Amidst swirling dimness and disorder,
vast and overflowing but not yet still.
The proper order is confused and replaced,
straightening my bearing and setting myself in order.
I set rules and guidelines as standards,
divining with my turtle-shell to seek understanding and reflection.
Gazing at where these chariots have withdrawn,
truly it is close, not far.
Was it for three years that none asked after me,
or for a single journey that there were nine returns?
I look back at the newly-risen sun,
racing across Qǔlíng and adorning my appearance.
The times scatter and drift,
I test the course of inevitable decay.
Releasing the broad and distant expanse,
accustomed to firm ties formed in frugality.
Circling to gather within Xiāngchéng,
reciting the remaining oath of purity and unity.
Soaked by wind and rain,
how dare I soar aloft or wander at leisure.
I secretly cherish unswerving constancy,
serene and unperturbed throughout all time.
How could lingering long move my feelings,
or altering my form for foreign lands?
Thus I choose a height to ascend as my perch,
and always delight joyously in peaceful well-being.
“Rhapsody on Shǒuyáng Mountain”
In the autumn of the first year of Zhèngyuán,
I was still a zhōngláng,
in the General-in-Chief’s mansion,
wandering alone beneath the southern wall,
with Shǒuyáng Mountain to the north,
thus I composed this rhapsody:
At the close of the year’s cycle,
the month’s beginning is shadowed by double gloom.
The wind [CH0F02A8] returns, twisting as it comes,
rain swirls and drenches the fine lapels of my robe.
Crickets chirp in the eastern chambers,
the tíjué calls in the western grove.
As dusk approaches I am companionless,
troubled and moved by sorrow.
Shaking the sand from my clothes, I step outside,
the ends of my sash lost and nowhere to be found.
I wander, leaning as distant thoughts arise,
with sighs and quiet humming.
Desiring to dress and venture forth,
yet all scoff and sneer at me.
Silent and lonely, I stand alone,
clearly upright yet without companions.
Harboring a heart once divided and alone,
loathe the false of the crowd who assail the true.
Trust can be realized and not abandoned,
better to soar high and escort oneself.
So I look up and gaze widely,
beholding the ridges of Shǒuyáng.
The dense groves flourish, leaning in clusters,
rustling and fresh as their sounds rise.
Descending is rough with no place to pause,
ascending is open, nowhere to cling.
The phoenix flies by without stopping,
while owls flock together and roost in unison.
Soaring away, distant and gone,
the two elders, destitute, return home.
Truly imprisoned and confined, dwelling here,
how is there leisure to dare criticize?
Esteemed grain is kept away, not possessed,
so death is sweet in gathering wild ferns.
Those turned from Yīn to follow Chāng,
casting themselves into peril and ruin without delay;
these advance but do not fit in,
then how could they be celebrated for benevolence and righteousness?
Indulging in long or short life without joy,
contending for censure and praise as their measure.
Observing past records if they truly are so,
how could these admirable words be worthy of longing?
If the Way is sought in what is minute,
why do you speak so grandly and at such length?
Let tranquility and emptiness guard the spirit,
how could one speak so ardently and extravagantly?
“Rhapsody on the Doves”
In the time of Jiāpíng, I acquired two young doves,
feeding them daily on millet and grain,
but later they were killed by a dog,
and so I composed this rhapsody for them.
In these blessed years of flourishing favor,
the great beginning is vague and dim, dispelling confusion.
There is a rare and fated bird,
akin to the calling dove in their kindred sound.
Soaring from carved trees, nesting in their corners,
building their high nests on distant pines;
breathing clouds and mist as they come and go,
wandering together beneath the morning sun,
after many days nurturing their offspring,
the seven young with fine appearance bring delight.
First they fold wings and grow their plumage,
then meet the autumn winds mournfully sighing.
Overturned and ruined, they find no rescue,
shaken and fallen, with none to aid.
Lingering above Huánshān with paced circling,
they gaze toward their old home, longing to enter;
crying in sadness to see each other off,
with grief for their parting, never to gather again.
In the end, alone and drifting,
grieved for the frail children, who tremble in fear.
Upon what trust can they rely for raising?
Rely on the closeness of brothers and kin.
Turning from the wild grass in search of virtue,
entrusting themselves to the gentleman’s tranquil room,
finding sweetness in the perfumed grain’s flavor,
at peace within the shuttered window, never falling ill.
With pure collars entwined, they embrace,
their splendor overflowing in radiant beauty,
their graceful forms refined as in a mirror,
pleased that their manners are always as one,
gently lowering their heads and raising them in ease,
seeking affection and favor day by day,
why must they long to fly away,
wishing only to give back and never to finish?
Caught by the mad dog in wild rage,
suffering cruel harm to their small bodies,
seeking escape but lost and fallen,
so cast aside and lost forever,
alas for the humble and base, worthy of lament,
how could even a moment be forgotten?
“Rhapsody on the Gibbon”
In former days, when Yǔ pacified the waters and ordered Yì to drive off the birds,
the rivers and valleys were cleansed and the mountains and forests combed,
thus spirits and strange beings took form on the Nine Tripods and wonders arrived in assembly.
So the fine fox and patterned leopard shed their pelts,
the tailed zōuyú offered their rarities,
Kuāfù and the solitary stag cleansed themselves of their pride,
the blue horse and the three zuī abandoned their herds:
these, in their strength, curtailed their lives.
As for the roaming of the xióngdàn along the river,
he is seen to accomplish his deeds by seizing danger;
Kuí, burdened by the abyss, acts according to his will,
Yáng Zhèn is renowned and wears fur.
Dwelling in solitude and sometimes appearing into light,
why does the secluded and hidden never follow suit?
The shǐ mouse, fearful of oppression, hides itself,
burrowing deep into the mysterious hills.
In the end, perhaps it is lured out in search of food:
who, by digging, can truly restrain it?
Indeed, if there is profit and desirability,
though rare in encounter, it still becomes prey.
Thus, those near do not count the years,
those afar do not mark the seasons,
the great ones may be remembered for ten thousand years,
the insignificant become a laughingstock before the eyes.
As for the monkey, it is but among the lesser of creatures,
yet still bound and chained among the lowly.
Its form is similar yet unlike,
its appearance diverges strangely but is not pure.
Outwardly clever in perception but lacking internal measure,
thus it has a human face but a beast's heart.
Its nature is narrow and superficial, striving for advancement,
like Hán Fēi imprisoned in Qín,
its brows raised in sudden agitation,
resembling artful words, false yet seemingly true.
The crowd of its followers is numerous,
just as felling trees leads to the loss of neighbors.
Straightening its robes and donning magnificent garments,
it harbors Sì Xiàng Wáng’s longing to return home.
Fond of desires and casting sidelong glances,
it has the elegant bearing of Cháng Qīng.
Lifting its head and lips to make postures,
its motions increase and constantly renew themselves.
It bathes in magnolia-scented waters yet grows filthy,
not the charm of Sòng Cháo’s captivating beauties.
Forever jesting and living in fetters,
though near in habit, it is not dear in heart.
With many talents and skills, what are they for?
Inevitably it suffers disgrace and its appearance is slighted.
Agile in form and fond of tricks,
it leaps high among cliffs and rocks.
Once darting eastward to evade through the woods,
it is found midway on the hills and pursued.
Bound and restricted by embroidered cords,
it looks back at the western mountains and longs for them.
It lingers along roof-beams with ease,
yet how could it forget Dèng Lín?
Hopes for the gentle favor of the noble lord,
displaying rare sights to exhaust its heart,
yet in the span of an instant to prolong the day,
how could it indulge in pleasure and self-admiration?
Thus it is doomed to die beneath the hall,
and forever perish in form and spirit.

“Qīng Sī Fù”
As I see it, what can be beheld of form,
is not the true beauty of color;
what can be heard of sound,
is not the true virtue of tone.
In ancient times, Huáng Dì ascended to immortality atop Jīng Shān,
stirring the Xián Chí on the south slope;
though spirits and deities are hidden,
yet even Kuí Yá could not hear their melodies.
The nǚwā radiated her glory on the eastern sea shore,
yet fluttered along the side of grand western waters;
the falling of forest and stone followed her,
yet the Yáo Tái did not reflect her light.
Therefore, subtle wonders lack form,
and in silence, without a sound,
only then can one behold the graceful and pure.
Thus, when the sun shines bright,
Jì Hòu does not parade her grace;
when bells and drums resound,
Yán Zǐ does not display his voice.
When clarity and emptiness are vast,
the spirits and marvelous creatures gather;
when drifting about in vagueness and illusion,
then the hidden depths are pierced and the darkness traversed.
With a heart pure as ice, a nature fine as jade,
then the thoughts are stirred to purity and remain.
In tranquility and absence of desire,
then one’s grand intentions find their comfort.
Ah, the thorough goodness of such intentions,
yet where could they dwell and not be fulfilled?
The cold wind passes over millet and grain,
instructing the fledgling waders in wandering.
Shēn Rú grieves as his mother returns,
Wú Hóng mourns as the elephant is born.
Such emotions stir and reach the numinous,
how could they surge and not strive?
When the mind does not intend yet the spirit is upright,
when the heart does not waver and remains sincere,
then abiding unity is practiced inwardly,
enduring like Yuè Zhǐ, unmoved.
Only at dawn clear and dusk peaceful,
pointing toward the misty expanse for lasting repose.
At this moment Xī Hé has already retired,
the dark night has just begun to close in,
Wàng Shū steadies the reins,
and the pale wind arises as his herald;
light curtains flutter endlessly,
splendid mats settle into purity;
Péng Pàng gently hums,
the mole cricket slowly sings.
Gazing at the towering southern mountains,
glancing at the verdant northern woods.
The great shade hides behind the rear chambers,
the bright moon shines on the front courtyard.
Then, stretching out and unable to sleep,
suddenly awakening with self-startled surprise.
How should one prolong the soul to attain tranquility,
and whether there will be a place to rest at the destination.
Thoughts drift and intent changes,
the heart trembles and stirs in reflection.
As if there is arrival that may be welcomed,
as if there is parting that does not require farewells.
Alas, contempt and lowliness cause loss of companionship,
emotions scatter and nothing is managed.
Can one truly perceive and see through reality,
indeed, like the clouds over Mèng, is it not so?
Amazed at the wondrous sound's unique crafting,
reflecting on the different colors present here.
Opening the qín and sè of cinnabar cassia,
listening to the uneven harmonies in Chóng Líng.
First singing softly with a faint resonance,
the emotions subtle and clever, winding and entwined.
Thus, summoning the clouds to bring forth breath,
thereby arousing great astonishment.
The sound whirls and surges boundlessly,
as if one stands atop Kūnlún looking toward the western seas;
leaping far, vast and boundless,
its ending cannot be determined.
The heart surges with no place to land,
thoughts travel far and are not even halfway returned,
Dèng Lín perishes in the great marshes,
Qīn Pī laments at the jade shore.
Wandering and hesitating,
elegant and widely extended.
Roaming the Plain Garden in endless prospect,
riding on the Huá Qí upon rushing waters.
Ever contemplating in pure devotion for lingering arrival,
clearing the broad thoroughfare with serene ease.
Following the open way for a straight path,
opening portals and passing freely through every chamber.
I envy the wondrous drifting and roaming,
leaning on the east wind to scatter radiance.
Bathing in the Wěi’s depths for inner purity,
the body cleansed and beyond reproach.
Disdaining white jade as a countenance,
donning rosy clouds for raiment.
Clad in the brilliance of the Nine Blossoms,
adorned with jade pendants that glimmer faintly.
Wearing shimmering garments that dazzle and scatter,
blending many hues in harmonious alignment.
Colors sparkling, flowing in brilliance,
intermingled and luxuriant in profusion.
Like morning clouds united in one gathering,
resembling changes which depend on one another;
beckoning the Lady of Ceremonies to lead the way,
instructing the Hé Nǚ to accompany her home.
Moving with ease yet advancing distinctly,
glancing between columns as she steps onto the stairs;
shaking the jade streamers and ringing the gems,
spreading the lilting sounds of Líng Yáng.
Treading the perilous tracks of Xiāo Shuǎng,
lightly stepping on the fleeting subtlety of separation.
Casting off the red shoes of Ān Cháo,
treading on woven mats, gathering at the curtained couch.
Spreading this arrival in the chamber,
now is the moment borne by drifting.
Fragrance wafts forth and is broadcast outward,
her lovely face shines with radiant beauty.
Clear words scent the air like orchids,
her speech gentle, never in discord.
Entrusting herself to the gathering of spirits,
floating in the lingering light of sun and moon.
Borrowing the pure essence of the subtle spirit,
how fortunate to embody grace and cherish oneself,
wishing to extend love for this evening,
yet still seeking what is right or wrong.
Cloaked in fragrance as the night unfolds,
intending to depart briefly yet return eternally.
Beholding joy yet not finding peace,
before words are finished the heart grieves.
Alas, how one may rely on clouds and rainbows,
then turning, spreading wings, soar aloft together.
Abandoning the crampedness of the central hall,
leaving behind the door and window, not residing therein.
Only curtains are stretched out yet there is no defense,
tables and mats are set but none support them.
Carried in a cloud-borne carriage shrouded in mist,
riding the twin dragons of Xiàhòu,
breaking off vermilion wood to shield from the sun,
raising a triple-layered zhī canopy,
winging lightly to the left and right,
floating softly and drifting gently.
Gazing at the morning glow in succession,
like a beautiful one harboring sorrow.
Gathering colors, intermingled to form patterns,
then suddenly dispersing and not lingering.
As if about to speak, yet words have not emerged,
again their atmosphere changes and drifts away.
As if hair hangs down, tresses lost,
ornaments not gathered and the form fading;
eyes look aside and depart of themselves,
intent to draw near but features recede.
Splendid and ornate, yet not brought to completion,
preceding the order of the old constellations.
Now when party and faction are rampant and darkness overcasts,
suddenly the old dwelling is unrecognized.
Ascending the lofty terrace of Huángyāo,
the thunder lord stirs, sending down rain.
Within are the brilliant and the long-lived,
scourging the outcasts and smiting the traitors.
Crushing demons and breaking spirits,
straightway ascending to the expected place.
Traveling the four quarters, giving the mind free rein,
who says I look back if some might doubt?
Soaring high, leaping and speeding swiftly,
to the northern pole and letting go.
Grasping the loose cord to show each other,
facing the cold gate and taking leave forever.
Since I do not trouble my heart with the myriad things,
how could a single woman be worthy of my thought!
Kàngfù Fù
“Kàngfù Fù”
I have once wandered to Kàngfù,
climbed its walls,
which bring forth sorrowful thoughts.
I composed this rhapsody to denounce it,
declaring it unworthy of joy.
As for Kàngfù,
it is the farthest land of the Nine Provinces,
a secluded emptiness from former ages.
Thus its city walls are low and cramped,
steep, narrow, not far-reaching;
its fields and lands are muddy and gradually silted,
bogged down and stagnant.
Its pools adjoin one another with water overflowing,
only foul plants grow abundantly, their fruit uneaten,
the earth below is gloomy and receives no harmonious qi,
the sun does not reach it fully, so its crops are not fine.
Thus its people are stubborn and perverse as táowù,
dull-witted and hard to transform.
Its territory is clogged and blocked, cut off and stopped,
divided and pressed by swirling depths,
its beginning and end closely linked,
root and tip entangled,
from of old till now,
ages have passed and years gone by.
Great lakes gather behind it,
boundaries of Qí lie ahead;
dikes and irrigation channels are not clear,
filth and turbidity have gathered in full,
the unworthy flock together,
houses empty of the virtuous.
Therefore its people are scattered and disorderly in their meals,
hiding in marshes and living in swamps,
their traces like elk and deer,
their ambitions fierce as tigers and leopards.
Thus its original soil is uncultivated,
trees and crops sparse and rare,
amaranth and reed choke its marshes,
mosquitoes and gnats torment the skin.
In those far and perilous places,
to the right is Jīnxiāng, to the left Gāopíng,
high mounds towering steeply,
deep streams rugged and jagged;
the beautiful kinds of things do not abide there,
only bears and tigers are born within,
thus the people suffer harm, being bitten and chewed,
bird and beast natures they possess.
In your nearer obstacles,
the cuckoo cries in the shade before it,
Qūchéng lies behind;
owls and hawks flock in mournful flight:
how could anyone have greater aspiration, even for a short while?
Thus its people have the nature of wolves and temper of jackals,
thundering and flashing without sincerity.
Looking southwards to Chūnshēn,
eastwards to Mèngcháng,
stretching towards the boundaries of Xuē city,
bordering Shànyáng;
there travelers passing in reverse lodge,
a hiding place for thieves and bandits.
Northward is Pínglù,
the western border of Qí;
a shortcut to Yān and Zhào,
an escape route for fugitives to linger at leisure;
so its people are reclusive and somewhat wayward,
hiding away and not forthright,
cherishing selfishness and embracing deceit,
thriving in false concealment,
ritual and morality unestablished,
simple customs not the same.
There remain the words of the former sages,
some crystal clear, others unheard.
How could a gentleman
linger in such a land!
“Memorial for Zhèng Chōng Advancing the Prince of Jìn”
Zhōng and the rest are guilty of a capital offense.
We respectfully notice the good tidings having illustriously arrived,
and privately hear that the illustrious lord persistently humbles himself.
Zhōng and the others earnestly yearn,
indeed with a foolish heart,
considering that the sage-kings set regulations,
that all generations should follow the same customs,
that virtue is honored and merit rewarded:
such practices have long existed.
In ancient times, Yī Yǐn,
simply a consort-retainer of Yǒuxīn,
assisted Chéng Tāng once,
and thus received the title “Āhēng”;
Duke Zhōugōng relied on the fortune already founded,
occupied an already secure holding,
made Qūfù radiant,
and claimed Guīmēng as his own;
Lǚ Shàng,
the fisherman of Pánxī,
at a single command,
was enfeoffed at Yíngqiū.
From that time hence,
those whose merits were slight but whose rewards were great are beyond number,
yet men of virtue and wisdom still consider it cause for praise.
How much more since the late Prime Minister,
whose house had manifest virtue through the generations,
supporting the House of Wèi,
thus maintaining the realm in peace,
with no flaws in government at court,
and the people voicing no reproach.
Previously, the illustrious lord campaigned west to Língzhōu,
reached north to the Shāmò,
from west of Yúzhōng,
all quaked in awe at your presence,
the Qiāng and Róng fled eastwards,
turning their gaze inward;
eastward you punished traitors and rebels,
the whole army victorious by your hand alone,
capturing the general of Hélǘ,
and cutting down the elite troops in their tens of thousands,
your authority reaching Nánhǎi,
your fame frightening the Triple Yuè;
within the borders, peace and security prevailed,
evils and malice did not arise,
so that foreign peoples feared your might,
and the Eastern Barbarians presented their dances.
Wherefore His Majesty reviewed the ceremonial statutes from of old,
established the state and made the residence illustrious,
proclaiming this Tàiyuán.
The illustrious lord should receive the imperial commission,
accept this great fortune,
and thus respond to Heaven and men.
The original achievements and grand feats are so dazzling;
the propitious happiness of the realm is so lofty.
Within and without all act in accord,
not veering, not disobeying.
Consequently, in campaigns,
you could cross the Jiāng in court robes,
sweep clear Wú and Huì;
blockade the upper Yangtze,
ascend Mount Mín for worship;
brandishing arms and lowering standards to command the world,
none afar but submit,
none nearby but are respectful,
making the virtue of mighty Wèi
shine beyond even that of Táng and Yú,
your illustrious exploits
surpass even those of Huán and Wén.
Then, gazing from Cāngzhōu to thank Zhī Bó,
climbing Jīshān to bow to Xǔ Yóu,
is this not splendid!
Supremely just and supremely fair,
none can be your peer.
Why persist in such excessive modesty!
We, Chōng and others, are not versed in the grand principles;
we dare to present our words for your consideration.

A Letter to Jìn Wén Wáng Recommending Lú Bō
*A Letter to Jìn Wén Wáng Recommending Lú Bō*
I have heard that to promote culture and aid governance
lies in acquiring the right people;
to gather the extraordinary and select the uncommon
is the lofty pursuit of sage-kings.
Thus the Eight Gentlemen went to Zhōu,
and the Way of Zhōu flourished;
when Shùn of Yú elevated the worthy,
Yuán Kǎi and others all served.
I respectfully consider that the illustrious lord, as duke and marquis,
is blessed by heaven with exceptional talent;
the Nine Virtues shine forth,
and he became advisor at the destined time,
propagating the Way and spreading civilization,
opening the four gates,
broadly extending his arms to worthy scholars with feathered wings
to assist in harmonious rule.
Therefore, brilliant men long to crowd the royal gates,
to record their names and commit themselves;
men like the Zhìzhì gather at the great office;
truly like Dènglín, Kūnwú, and soaring phoenixes coming to roost;
Xuánlí blending in the market,
and the drooping thorn gathering the assembly.
I have humbly observed the assistant administrator of my humble province,
my fellow countryman Lú Bō,
aged thirty-two,
styled Jǐngxuān.
From youth, he has shown uncommon talent and excellence;
grown up, he possesses magnanimity and virtue;
fond of the Way, delighted in propriety,
upholding righteousness and relying on benevolence;
diligently studying the classics and canons,
ascending to the hall and seeing what is profound;
intelligent and discerning the principles of things,
his mind understanding subtleties.
Steadfast and upright, capable of managing affairs;
loyal and respectful, able to uphold the court;
clear in judgment, able to resolve doubts;
resourceful and prudent, able to respond as needed.
When faced with difficulty, he is not confused;
in urgent matters, his clarity increases.
If allowed to assist in governing and managing affairs,
he is a vessel for administration;
entrusted with diplomatic duties,
he is suited for representation.
Immersed in learning and records,
he is a model in literature;
eloquent in compositions and narratives,
an exemplar among excellent historians.
Yet his studies are not done for recognition,
nor his conduct for advancement;
thus, he has long been submerged and obscure,
not yet reached the highest offices.
Truly, he is an outstanding figure from humble origins,
an effective instrument of his time;
he ought to be honored with a distinguished post,
to harmonize flavors in the great cauldron.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Where there is praise,
there must be testing."
What Lú Bō can do
is demonstrated by present achievements.
He does not dare to boast falsely,
seeking fame in the great office.

A Letter in Reply to Fú Yì
Jí expresses the following:
I have heard your words and read your intentions,
and my heart is moved by your written traces.
The height of the nine heavens,
even swift wings cannot reach its summit;
the depth of the four seas,
hidden fish cannot fathom its bottom;
how could the judgments of one without even hair or feathers discuss such things!
Moreover, the dark cloud has no fixed form;
the flying dragon has no constant shape:
sometimes it crosses the river in the morning and vanishes by evening,
flourishing and declining in an instant;
sometimes it wallows in the mud and soars to the heavens,
descending in the morning, ascending at night,
when it lets itself expand, even eight directions are insufficient to encompass its tracks,
when it contracts, there is no space for ease;
this too cannot be observed by the blind,
nor understood by small insects.
Thus, those whose learning is broad and profound
cannot be thoroughly comprehended by superficial effort;
those with numinous transformation and divine subtlety
cannot be discerned by petty vessels.
Why then do you, good sir, trouble yourself with such zeal and seek so diligently from me!
Men's abilities and circumstances cannot be made equal,
their preferences and aspirations differ.
Luán and fèng soar in the clouds, dancing with their wings,
while the dove and yuān delight in the bramble forest, flying at leisure;
the chī swims along the eight shores to cleanse its scales,
while the turtle frolics in the shallow pools and travels with its kind;
thus each follows his own passion to seek joy.
Judging this by that,
how can they be made the same?
As for the establishment of virtue in people,
it is as if one extends a net to encompass the world;
how could one merely be reserved and enter the snare?
It is to open the mold to shape the customs;
when would there be leisure to destroy one's substance only to meet regulations?
If good fortune has not yet harmonized,
and the divine mechanism has no standard,
then the spirit soars and the will resists,
rising high above the world,
the essence sweeping forth beyond the limits of the mysterious realm,
unfurling wondrous virtue beyond the ninefold bounds, soaring on the radiance and leaping with vigor,
vaulting over the heights and suddenly vanishing,
at ease, changing together with the Way,
free and untrammeled, flowing alongside the sun and moon,
joining with the void to be equal to transformation,
meeting with yīngqí to match in transformation,
rising above what is highest,
descending below what is lowest,
dwelling in what is without a dwelling,
emerging from what is without a gate,
making the coming and going of all things equal,
following the waxing and waning of the six vital energies,
gathering the mysterious net at the Grand Ultimate,
caressing the oneness of Heaven in the vast emptiness,
floating dust cannot stir its waves,
flying particles cannot defile its purity,
it merely temporarily lodges the body in this domain,
how can its spirit and clarity be discerned?
Though its achievements are heard of without exception,
and its reputation is praised without omission,
yet if its illumination reaches some,
it is no wonder.
Consider the approach of the junzi:
wishing to display gold able to topple a city,
yet seeking to sell it for a hundred coins;
crafting the rituals of Heaven,
but imitating the measures of inches of skin;
fatiguing the king's own person to manage affairs,
upholding the foul and filthy to complete oneself;
sinking into the shallow traces of oxen,
and resenting that the Milky Way has no roots;
how shameful is such pettiness,
how lamentable such affairs.
Truly their strategies deviate by far,
and surely the great Dao is grand and profound;
yet they walk only on the common roads,
never thinking far and thus vexing themselves.
Their afflictions are many and confused,
and their efforts at explanation are few.
Ruǎn Jí respectfully submits.
