"Discourse on the Comprehensiveness of the Yì"
Ruǎn Zǐ said:
What is the Yì?
It is the mysterious truth of old,
the classic of change from ancient times.
In the time of Pāoxī Shì, when Heaven and Earth had completed one cycle,
and all living things were worn and withered,
useful means did not exist,
regulations and systems were obscure and indistinct,
the virtue of numinous clarity was not communicated,
and the affections of ten thousand ages were not of the same kind;
thus there began the creation of the Eight Trigrams.
Drawing them forth and extending them,
touching categories to make them grow,
dividing yīn and yáng,
arranging firmness and gentleness,
assembling mountains and marshes,
connecting water and fire,
blending them into one,
transforming them to make them communicate,
ending with Wèi Jì,
the sixty-four trigrams are exhausted yet inexhaustible.
Thus Heaven and Earth take form and all creatures take shape,
good and ill become manifest and repentance and shame arise,
affairs have their uses,
transformation has its completion.
Sitting facing south and listening to judgments,
governing by turning toward the light;
tying knots in cords to make nets and snares,
obtaining the commodities of midday,
cultivating the benefits of the plow to teach,
all under Heaven thereby attained their proper places.
Huáng Dì, Yáo, and Shùn all responded to the needs of their times,
each having something to draw upon,
exhausting the spirits to understand transformation,
and expounding in accord with the celestial order.
Pāoxī Shì set forth the transformations of the sixty-four trigrams;
later sages observed and followed them,
modeling them and applying them.
The classic records of Yǔ and Tāng all remain,
but the writings of high antiquity do not survive;
when it came to Wén Wáng,
thus he appended their words,
and thus the Guīcáng lineage faded away and the Zhōu canonical classics arose.
Above and below were not fixed,
hardness and softness changed places,
and they could not serve as unchanging standards,
for change follows what is appropriate,
therefore it is called "Yì" ("Change").
The Yì as a book
is rooted in Tiāndì,
follows Yīnyáng,
infers waxing and waning,
and emerges from what is hidden and subtle to reach what is evident and manifest.
Thus, at the beginning of Qián Yuán, "The hidden dragon should not act,"
speaks of the virtue of the great person being concealed and not yet revealed,
hidden and not yet accomplished,
waiting for the proper time to rise,
responding to change to manifest.
Once Heaven and Earth are established,
Zhūn and Méng arise,
waiting with patience for the right time,
litigation establishes justice,
leaders gather the masses,
harmonizing brings peace to the people;
thus, "the Former Kings established ten thousand states,
and drew the lords near,"
gathering their hearts.
Primordially accumulating,
sustaining and regulating,
thus upper and lower are in harmony,
"shaping and perfecting the Way of Heaven and Earth,
assisting and complementing the needs of Heaven and Earth to manage the people,"
following their proper order.
When the Former Kings passed away,
virtue and law drifted apart,
superiors encroached and inferiors were debased,
ruler and minister were not restrained,
firm and yielding were not in harmony,
Heaven and Earth did not commune;
thus the noble pursues unity among like kinds,
restraining evil and promoting good,
to achieve greatness.
Modesty yet shining forth,
taking from the many to benefit the few,
exalting sages and the worthy to empower,
thunder arises from the earth;
then the great person attains position,
and the enlightened and sage arise anew.
Thus the Former Kings created music to honor Shàngdì,
clearly illuminating the Way to repay Heaven’s blessing.
Hereupon all things submit,
follow and serve;
the son follows the father,
the minister succeeds the ruler,
taking charge and unifying authority,
observing all under Heaven in grand perspective.
Thus the Former Kings investigated the regions and observed the people, establishing teaching,
setting models by measuring.
Embracing and possessing them,
gathering them together in inclusion,
thus the Former Kings used them to clarify punishments and regulate laws.
From above downwards,
the noble reveres the humble,
beauty is fulfilled, success is attained;
when the time is extreme and the sun at its height,
the Former Kings close the passes,
merchants and travelers do not move,
the sovereign does not survey the regions,
to quiet the people.
When the latter generations declined,
it was not through scheming that they gained,
but responding to times and following Heaven,
not acting capriciously;
thus the Former Kings flourished in adapting to the times and nurtured all beings,
dispensing kindness and bestowing grace to establish their virtue.
All creatures return and follow,
as the law flows and is inherited,
cultivating good and rectifying evil,
benefit accumulating brings forth harm,
when firmness exceeds its bounds one loses command,
habitually being endangered in order and rank,
those above lose their Way,
those below lose their groups.
Hereupon the great person continues the illumination,
shining upon the four quarters,
revealing his virtue.
From Qián Yuán onwards,
the effect is peaceful and clear,
prosperity and decline each have their time,
firmness and yielding are without constancy,
sometimes gained, sometimes lost,
one Yīn, one Yáng,
going out and coming in, auspicious or inauspicious,
from what is obscure perceiving what is manifest;
refinement and clarity find their limit,
with wings but not flying,
following then remaining,
those who take are returned,
those who give act accordingly,
use lies in what is subtle,
valuing change and caution in the small,
pursuing things in mutual accord;
none but those who know how both to hide what is to come and store what is past can discern it.
The Yì as a book
covers the Way of Heaven and Earth,
embraces the conditions of all things.
When the Way reaches its utmost, it returns;
when events reach their extreme, they change.
"Return" is used to respond to the time;
"change" is used to address pressing affairs.
By responding to the time,
all under Heaven longs for its beneficence;
by acting in pressing affairs,
all things rely on its advantages.
When beneficence is given, all under Heaven yields;
this is why all under Heaven obeys Nature,
and brings favor to all living beings.
Wealth and nobility equal to Heaven and Earth,
merit and fame filling the Six Directions,
none can overturn it,
none can harm it,
for the Way does not run counter to itself.
Heaven and Earth
are the masters of the Yì;
the myriad things
are the heart of the Yì.
Therefore, one receives with emptiness,
and responds with harmony.
Male below, female above,
conveying their energies;
the yielding embraces the firm,
so their kind endures long;
to proceed with compliance and hold it,
to retreat with withdrawal.
Above raised high, below piled up,
the firm moves with great strength.
Rectitude and greatness must be used;
when power flourishes, it is looked to;
when clarity rises, only then does it advance;
when it shines greatly, it is wounded.
To gather and place oneself,
to distinguish and form kinds.
When separation and estrangement are dissolved,
remissness results in loss.
The time for decrease and increase comes in turns,
examine to govern and direct.
Proclaim in the royal court,
ride in a chariot of five horses and meet defeat.
When the firm has decided, the yielding,
above seeks, below unites;
a minister meets an enlightened lord,
the yielding encounters the firm,
all categories are smooth and functioning.
When the firm is centered and upright,
the world proceeds greatly;
therefore, afterward, carry out the commands and grant decrees to the Four States,
thus honoring the teachings on separation.
Then Heaven and Earth assemble together,
the people combine their efforts,
rise without cease,
reach the extreme and return below,
as a well provides endlessly;
the low cannot communicate,
it is impossible not to change.
To change is to shape instruments;
honor and humility are divided in measure,
elders and juniors have their order.
Rule with thunder,
guard with awe.
Movement cannot be endless;
the opponent responds and acts.
Gradually advance,
to seek position for a person
is the junzǐ’s desire for advancement.
A minister seeks his lord,
yīn follows yáng,
entrust and return with sincerity,
thus obtaining their proper place.
Return and respond,
focus and unite,
the virtues of yáng receive the return,
the Way is ample and ranks great.
Worthy people and junzǐ,
accomplish greatness with the masses.
Extremes of poverty and extravagance lose the position of dàfū;
gathered together and without accommodation,
even with accommodation, there is nowhere.
Humble oneself, lower the mind,
it is beneficial to see great people.
Comply to extend the command,
the yielding is submissive to the firm.
Enter and persuade,
persuade and teach,
follow and respond to others.
Clearly formed with brilliance,
like wind moves above water;
possessing pattern and radiance,
the male's action is inexhaustible,
the female's position is outside;
the multitude of yīn supports the fifth,
above matches the center,
beginning anew from the start,
riding wood achieves merit,
so the Former Kings made offerings to Dì,
established ancestral temples,
and served Heaven by founding states.
Firmness and yielding are divided in proper measure,
regulated with moderation,
its Way is inexhaustible.
Trust and love unite within,
the firm attains the central position,
sincerity arises from the heart,
and the myriad beings align each to their kind.
When gain is too great, it diminishes;
when one goes too far, it becomes excessive;
responding to what is distant,
in silence there is no advantage;
therefore the junzǐ acts with reverence in conduct,
mourns deeply in loss,
is sincere, not false, and sparing with his pretenses.
Small excess is lower than tài,
not fitting above;
below halts, above moves,
there is the image of flying birds.
In the beginning, liù is below kǎn,
shàng liù in the body of lí,
flying birds bring misfortune,
thus there are calamities and disasters.
Yielding takes the center,
the firm loses its place,
to act in timely advantage,
to go too far and wish to proceed,
is the sign of small success;
all yīn rides on yáng,
firm yáng is replaced and superseded,
lord and minister trade places,
disorder prevails without end,
this is not called the center.
Therefore the junzǐ considers trouble and prepares in advance,
and plans against its ruin.
Transformation is inexhaustible,
failure cycles to beginning again,
the firm has not yet emerged,
yīn dwells at the center,
the yielding assists and nothing is neglected,
thus it crosses over without limit,
thus resembling the Hé Luò,
where the spirit-beings instruct and all under Heaven yields.
Discriminating carefully in position,
yīn and yáng seek each other,
the beginning shares the Way,
and creates a distant basis.
The structure of the hexagrams opens and closes;
Qián opens with one,
Kūn closes with two.
When Qián and Kūn form their structure, firmness and gentleness are each in their position;
thus wood withers in Wèi,
water is born in Shēn,
and Kūn is in the southwest.
Fire withers in Xū,
wood is born in Hài,
and Qián is in the northwest.
This is the juncture of firm and yielding;
thus they are called father and mother.
Yang receives from Zhèn's movement,
initiates and continues in succession,
acts decisively and proceeds forward,
and all things flourish;
thus it is called the eldest son.
Water withers in Chén,
metal is born in Sì,
a single qi preserves it,
ending and then rising again,
thus Xùn is the eldest daughter.
Zhèn arises in wind,
the virtue of yin has its order,
in fire the cuckoo sings,
the way of the mother is soon to begin,
thus Lí is the middle daughter.
Again, in the northwest,
vigorous and ready for battle about to ascend,
the youngest yin is childlike and uncomprehending,
declining and unable to prevail,
thus Duì is the youngest daughter.
In the granary, extracting and leaving,
the beginning of the profound is yang,
in the middle but not yet reached,
contained but not yet manifest,
thus Kǎn is the middle son.
Circulating and joining together,
all things having ended,
producing the subtleties anew,
bright but not yet harmonized,
thus Gèn is the youngest son.
Qián is round, Kūn is square,
the female is gentle, the male is firm,
motion between strength and gentleness is timely,
and fortune or misfortune is thus determined.
Following transformation, one comes to understand life;
from change, one witnesses disappearance.
Thus, fortune and misfortune, success and failure,
must not be confused.
What is Dàguò?
The ridgepole bends and none support it,
it is an excess among the great.
When the Former Kings governed the world,
punishments were established but not transgressed,
penalties were set forth but not implemented,
they became acquainted with Kǎn, firm and central,
and relied on an open heart.
The king rectified his virtue,
the duke kept to his charge,
upper and lower had no doubts,
ministers and ruler were without confusion.
Bringing in the agreement through the window;
if not by the door, what harm is there?
Chariots and riders through the central gate,
swords and halberds at the threshold,
though placed among brambles,
misfortune continues for three years;
the top six loses the way,
punishment is carried out.
Thus Gāozōng attacked Guǐfāng,
employing gentleness at the center;
after three years, there was reward,
and so virtue became abundant.
The five announcements in Tóngrén,
consider their conclusion;
the excellence at the end of Lǚ,
delights in its completion.
Thus those who lose in punishment are severe but lack control,
those who lose virtue are exalted but not honored;
thus the noble man holds position by uprightness,
strengthens law to awe the people.
What is permitted brings smoothness,
but to deafen oneself brings misfortune.
What is Xiǎoguò?
Overstepping position and overbearing the superior,
harming what is right, endangering the self,
it is the excess of the small.
Why is disorder the outcome of the beginning nine in Jìjì?
Water above the sun,
three yins ride above yang,
seeking completion by force,
not stopping will lead to ruin,
thus it is first auspicious and ending in disorder.
For the upper six in Wèijì,
drinking wine brings no harm,
why?
Going too far but not amending,
being in danger but not cautious,
who will blame it?
What is Wúwàng?
Arriving without expectation,
it is not the opposition and union of yin and yang acting contrary.
Six in the third place,
the calamity of Wúwàng,
perhaps ties it to the ox,
a traveler encounters it,
the townsman suffers calamity,
why?
Having a country but not gathering its people,
having a multitude but not maintaining its tools,
so the traveler gains it,
is that not a disaster?
The illness of nine in the fifth place should not be treated with medicine,
why?
Because the extraordinary is abundant,
leaving it to be alike,
the illness of Wúwàng,
disaster removes misfortune,
success and failure are determined by Heaven’s timing,
what merit has the sickness?
Not treating it brings joy,
if not accomplished, what discernment is there?
What is the dragon?
It is a type symbolizing vigorous yang,
a metaphor for great virtue and supreme honor.
It represents the fullness of Heaven,
indicating that in great virtue, none surpasses supreme honor.
When a great person receives the mandate,
residing in the center and confronting the sun,
this is the utmost of virtue.
Why does the exalted dragon have regret?
Because he sustains his honor by inheritance,
but, relying on circumstance, his virtue is not complete.
He desires greatness but does not attend to what is small,
indulges in extravagance but does not think of lack,
resides rightly in a high position without humility,
enjoys honor and labors but lacks true foundation,
losing his will and endangering his person,
thus comes regret.
What is the “former king”?
It is the achievement of the great person.
Therefore, he founded the myriad states,
befriended the zhūhóu,
and established righteousness;
he created music to offer to Shàngdì,
and rectified the mandate;
inspected the directions and observed the people,
thus promulgating his decrees;
clarified punishments and instructed in laws,
supervised the administration;
closed the passes and did not travel,
thereby calming the troubled people;
cultivated at proper times and nurtured virtue,
thus ensuring manifest blessings;
sacrificed to the Emperor and established temples,
thereby displaying his rewards.
To say it was accomplished by the shèngwáng,
is not to say it was during times of peace alone.
What is the “empress”?
She completes the prince and establishes his position,
inherits the enterprise and perfects the institutions,
preserves the teaching and guards the laws,
nurtures and administers so as to ensure order and peace.
Therefore, naturally all is accomplished and used,
so that the highest degree of harmony is achieved.
The empress fulfills the Way of Heaven and Earth to aid the people.
She perfects the transformations and governs judgments,
publishes orders and prescribes regulations,
and continues the unbroken lineage during decline.
She occupies the center, managing the essential affairs,
not simply acting as one who newly receives the mandate.
What is the “superior”?
Sun and moon alternate,
prosperity and decline succeed each other;
if abundance is sought too ornately, prosperity will not endure.
Therefore, neither king nor empress lays claim,
nor does the junzǐ err,
the superior enriches the inferior,
such is the Way of nature.
What is the junzǐ?
He assists the sage and supports the mandate,
helps in teaching and clarifies the law,
observes the times and acts,
with the Way he serves others as minister.
He governs his conduct by upright virtue,
guards himself by discerning danger and decline,
therefore, he organizes and rectifies abundance,
acts resolutely to fulfill righteousness,
takes food and drink according to the season,
distinguishes rightness to effect his actions,
all in order to exemplify the state-building of the former kings,
and to assist the shèngrén with spirit and will.
He perceives danger, considers difficulties,
anticipates calamity to prepare against it,
distinguishes things and keeps to his bounds,
is cautious at the beginning and reverent when starting,
all these are the conduct of ministers,
not the Way of the great prince.
What is the great person?
He possesses the dragon’s virtue, hidden yet achieved,
illuminating both noble and base,
having position without self-assertion,
acting out of greatness.
Therefore, when exceeding he eliminates and manifests to all, illuminating what was hidden;
the great person shines forth with renewed brilliance,
continuing to radiate in all directions,
and all things look up and receive life.
He joins his virtue with Heaven and Earth,
achieving without striving,
therefore, the great person transforms like the tiger,
and enlivens the virtue of Heaven.
The junzǐ says:
"The Yì,
follows Heaven and Earth,
orders the myriad things,
where the square and the circle have proper forms,
and the four seasons their constant positions,
matters and achievements have their attachment,
birds and beasts their assembling;
therefore, nothing among the myriad things is not one.
From yīn and yáng nature is born,
and so there is firmness and gentleness;
from firmness and gentleness comes emotion,
and from emotion comes love and hate.
From love and hate arise gain and loss,
from gain and loss come regret and shame,
and as regret and shame are made manifest, so are auspiciousness and misfortune revealed.
The eight trigrams occupy their positions to rectify nature,
and the milfoil and tortoise, being round and responsive, investigate emotion.
When emotion and nature meet, then benefit and harm are revealed.
Thus, benevolence and righteousness are established to fix nature,
the milfoil and tortoise are used to regulate emotion.
Where benevolence and righteousness are paired, misfortune and fortune are distinguished.
Therefore, the sage establishes the basis of all things under Heaven,
fixes the order of honor and base,
aligns the balance of yīn and yáng,
and distinguishes the degrees of firmness and gentleness.
Those who follow thrive,
those who oppose perish,
those who gain it are secure in body,
those who lose it are endangered.
Therefore, those who transgress in seeking difference,
though they may meet good fortune, disaster will surely come;
while those who know and firmly maintain,
though pressed to extremity, will surely attain harmony.
Thus isolation is the root of virtue,
and wantonness the source of harm;
progression is a return to the beginning,
completion stems from the root of beginning.
Therefore, what has not yet arrived cannot be forced open,
what has already been used cannot be overstepped.
Zhòu possessed the title of Son of Heaven,
but was the peer of commoners,
lived near Zhōu, a minor lord,
but enjoyed the role of a guest at Xīshān.
The correspondence of inner and outer had already taken effect,
yet honor and base were not yet distinguished—
why was this?
Because the Way of Heaven was not exhausted,
and good and evil were not yet pure.
Therefore, those who understand the Way of Heaven do not desire,
those discerning in human virtue do not worry.
When in high position, they do not oppress those below;
when in a humble place, they do not violate those above.
Therefore, the Way cannot be opposed,
nor can virtue be contravened.
Thus, the sage stands alone without distress,
the multitude brings no benefit,
releasing it, the Way remains,
using it, it cannot be exhausted.
From this it can be seen,
the Yì is thereby made transparent.
“On Penetrating Lǎo”
The sage understands the principles of Heaven and Man,
is versed in the boundaries of nature,
penetrates the essence of government and transformation,
and is clear in the instructions of great caution.
Thus the ruler and minister rule with arms folded,
preserving the simple uncarved nature of the Grand Origin,
the hundred clans rejoice peacefully, maintaining the balance of life and nature.
○ “Imperial Readings” One.
The Way—
following nature as law and acting accordingly—
if marquises and kings can preserve it,
all things will transform of themselves.
The Yì calls it “Tàijí,”
Chūnqiū calls it “Yuán,”
Lǎozi calls it “Dào.”
○ “Imperial Readings” One.
The Three Sovereigns depended on the Way;
the Five Emperors relied on virtue;
the Three Kings exercised benevolence;
the Five Hegemons acted through righteousness;
powerful states depended on intelligence—
these are the distinctions of superiority and inferiority,
and the varying degrees of abundance and scarcity.
○ “Imperial Readings” Seventy-Seven.
“Discourse on Attaining Zhuāng”
In the time of Yīdānyān,
in the year of Zhíxú,
when all things were just beginning,
in the month of long nights in late autumn,
the master paced and soared,
roamed riding the wind,
traveled beside the Rèshuǐ,
ascended the hills of Yǐnbèn,
stood by the winding Yuán path,
looked back at the land of Yāngmǎng,
suddenly stood motionless,
abruptly came to rest,
not knowing why he had traveled before,
nor why he lingered now;
regretful, he knew no joy,
somberly he returned alone in white.
At midday, in leisure,
he leaned on his armrest and played the qín.
So the Jìnshēn gentlemen and lovers of the extraordinary, upon hearing of this together,
gathered to discuss and craft words and phrases,
to address their longstanding doubts.
Thus, they tidied their robes and arranged their attire,
ground their teeth in anticipation,
pressing forward with the weight of years,
following one another in succession.
They walked with a shining demeanor,
casting wide and searching glances,
stepping up and mounting the stairs,
hurrying and soaring to the place.
They sat shoulder to shoulder,
folded their sleeves respectfully and restrained themselves,
hesitated and looked at one another,
none willing to speak first.
There was one among them,
who was the champion and outstanding figure;
with angry eyes and a forceful manner, he loudly declared:
“I was born after the times of Tāng and Yú,
grew up as a descendant of Wén and Wǔ,
thrived in the flourishing age of Chéng and Kāng,
live in the abundance of this present era,
recite the teachings of the Six Classics,
and practice the ways of our scholars.
Donning sand-colored robes,
wearing hats with soaring wings,
letting long, curved skirts hang down,
raising the double yì sleeves for many a day;
yet I have not heard the essentials of the ultimate Way,
and what makes it different here!
The great ones praise it,
the lesser ones follow it.
I wish to hear the ultimate teachings,
so as to resolve my doubts.”
The Master said:
“What is it,
that you doubt?”
The guest said:
“The Way of Heaven esteems life,
the Way of Earth esteems steadfastness.
The sages cultivate these,
to establish their renown.
Auspiciousness and misfortune have their allotments,
right and wrong have their standards.
People pursue benefit and seek high position,
hate death and value life;
thus the world is at peace and great deeds are accomplished.
Now Zhuāng Zhōu treats calamity and fortune alike, and sees life and death as one;
takes Heaven and Earth as one thing,
and all beings as a single finger.
Is this not a delusion that veils the truth,
and yet believes itself sincere?”
At this, the Master calmly laid his hand upon the qín,
sighed deeply and with emotion,
looked downward and smiled slightly,
looked upward and gazed afar,
drew in and let out his vital breath,
and said what he saw:
“In the past, there was one who wished to view from atop Làng Fēng;
equipped himself with fine robes and official cap,
rode a magnificent huáliú horse,
but arrived only at the foot of Kūnlún,
and perished without return.
The official cap,
is merely decorum of attire;
the huáliú horse,
is but an ordinary steed;
they are not means to fly over the walls of Zēngchéng,
or to wander within Xuánpǔ.
Moreover, even Zhúlóng’s light,
does not illuminate every hall;
and the mouth of Tángshān,
does not discourse within winding chambers.
Today, as I prepare to cast aside these lofty heights,
cease the flow of falsehoods,
and speak of the path you follow,
perhaps you will awaken and attain what is near!
Heaven and Earth arise from zìrán (spontaneity);
the myriad beings arise from Heaven and Earth.
That which is spontaneous has no outside,
thus Heaven and Earth are named;
Heaven and Earth have an inside,
thus the myriad things are born.
When there is no outside,
who can say things are different?
When there is an inside,
who can say things are distinct?
The earth moves its dryness,
the heavens bear their moisture.
The moon comes forth in the east,
the sun sets in the west,
each following the other,
separating to unite again.
Rising is called yáng,
descending is called yīn.
Within earth, it is called principle;
within heaven, it is called pattern.
Gathered, it is called rain;
dispersed, it is called wind.
When hot, it is called fire;
when solidified, ice.
Given form, it is stone;
given semblance, stars.
At the new moon, day begins;
at the dark, it is night.
Flowing, it is river;
turning, it is abyss.
Level, it is plain;
piled up, it is mountain.
Male and female occupy equal positions,
mountains and marshes breathe together,
thunder and wind do not clash directly,
water and fire do not attack each other.
Heaven and Earth unite their virtue,
the sun and moon follow their light,
spontaneity is one body,
thus all beings follow their constant.
Going in is called yōu (inner mystery),
coming out is called zhāng (manifestation);
one vital energy waxing and waning,
transforming without harm.
Therefore, when thunder and lightning come from heavy yīn,
they do not arise from different origins.
Heaven, earth, sun, and moon,
are not separate things.
Thus it is said:
From a standpoint of difference,
the liver and gallbladder are as distant as Chǔ and Yuè;
from a standpoint of unity,
all things are one body.
Man lives between Heaven and Earth,
endowed with the form of spontaneity.
The body,
is the essential energy of yīn and yáng.
Nature,
is the true character of the five elements;
Emotion,
is the changeable longing of the wandering soul;
Spirit,
is that by which Heaven and Earth govern.
If viewed by life,
nothing is not long-lived;
viewed by death,
nothing is not short-lived.
From the small perspective,
all things are small;
from the great perspective,
all things are large.
For Shāngzi to be considered long-lived,
and Péngzǔ to be considered short-lived;
for an autumn hair to be great,
and Tàishān to be small;
thus, to see life and death as a single thread,
and right and wrong as a single strand.
Speak of them separately,
and beard and eyebrows have different names;
discuss them as one,
and they are but a single hair of the body.
The words of the Six Classics,
are teachings of distinction;
the words of Zhuāng Zhōu,
are expressions of meaning.
Contemplate on a large scale,
and the utmost has no outside;
on a small scale,
things have their limits.
To keep the tally of tens and fives,
and discern the names of right and left,
is but a partial discourse;
to follow spontaneity,
and dwell within Heaven and Earth,
is the boundless discussion.
As for the desires of ear and eye,
and the application of ranks,
holding office without changing one’s role,
and satisfying oneself,
is not to sever hands and feet,
or to tear the body apart.
Yet, those who delight in difference in later ages do not look to the root,
each only speaks for himself,
why wait for others?
Truncating life and harming nature,
turning themselves into enemies,
dismembering the body,
and feeling no pain;
looking at colors and neglecting what the ears hear,
the ears listen and do not wait for the heart’s thought,
the mind chases desires and does not rest in what the nature enjoys,
therefore when sickness arises, life is incomplete;
when disaster and chaos appear, all beings are left damaged.
As for the perfected person,
he is at ease in life and tranquil in death.
When one is at ease in life, his feelings are not confused;
when one is tranquil in death, his spirit does not depart.
Thus he is able to transform with yīn-yáng without change,
and follow the transformations of Heaven and Earth without being moved.
He exhausts his lifespan in life,
follows what is fitting in death,
his mind and vital energies are level and well ordered,
neither dissipating nor lacking.
Therefore Guǎngchéngzǐ dwelt on Kōngtóng Mountain to enter the limitless gate,
and Xuānyuán ascended Kūnlún Hill, leaving behind the root of the mysterious pearl.
This is why those who conceal their persons find it easy to survive,
while those who abandon their origins find it hard to last forever.
If Féng Yí had not met Hǎiruò,
he would not have considered himself small;
if the clouds were never lost in dim vastness,
they would have no way to know their own minuteness.
From this, we may say:
Those who affirm themselves are not illustrious;
those who establish themselves do not stand;
those who guard what they possess have a basis;
those who cling to what they do not have have nothing to hold.
When the moon is a crescent, it will become full;
the sun at dawn shall be followed;
the Xiánchí does not linger above Yánggǔ,
and after a suspended chariot comes entry.
Therefore, those who seek gain lose;
those who contend for clarity fail;
those without desire are naturally content;
those who are empty receive fullness.
That the mountain is tranquil and the valley deep
is the Way of Nature;
to attain the Way and rectify oneself
is the substance of the jūnzǐ.
Thus, those who create cleverness and craft bring harm to things,
those who clarify right and wrong endanger themselves,
those who embellish themselves to display purity are confused by life,
those who fear death and revere life lose their constancy.
Thus, if the principle of nature cannot be enacted,
Heaven and Earth are not harmonious, and sun and moon contend to follow;
morning and evening lose their times, and day and night have no distinction;
competition in pursuit of profit,
disorder and reckless galloping,
father and son are not in harmony,
ruler and minister become estranged.
Those who repeat words to seek credibility
possess only the sincerity of the bridge's underside;
those who conquer themselves to benefit others
hold only the benevolence outside the city walls;
those who steal the pheasant's warp
are sons who bring their families to ruin;
those who cut open their bellies and slice their flesh
are ministers who bring disorder to their states;
those who display brilliance and radiance,
who cloak themselves in dew and vapor,
are scholars of a benighted age;
those who walk upon frost and dew,
who are covered in dust and dirt,
are the people of greed and rapacity;
those who purify themselves to blame the world,
those who cultivate themselves to clarify murkiness and blame others are all such as slander;
those who constantly speak of right and wrong,
who turn from substance to chase ornamentation,
are the deluded sort;
how can sincerity be currying favor,
or seeking trust by appearances?
Therefore, those who don pearls and jade to rush into fire and water
meet the end of Jié and Zhòu;
those who bear beans and gather ferns,
yet die of hunger,
share the poverty of Yán Yí.
Thus, when the roads to fame and profit are open,
the sincerity of loyalty and trust thins;
when the disputes about right and wrong are made manifest,
the feelings of simplicity and honesty are consumed.
Therefore, the utmost of the Supreme Way
is the mixing and unifying of all, undivided;
all are one body,
no word of gain or loss is heard.
Fúxīshì tied cords;
Shénnóng taught farming;
those who opposed them died,
those who conformed lived.
But how can we truly know that greed for murkiness is punishment
and chasteness and purity is fame?
Let the essentials of perfect virtue
have nothing outside them, and that is all.
The great equilibrium is pure and firm,
never divided from its source;
clear, tranquil, silent, and solitary,
hollow and expansive and waiting,
virtue and evil are not divided there,
right and wrong are nowhere contended;
thus, all things return to what they are and obtain their true natures.
After Rú and Mò,
the “hard and white” dispute together arose;
fortune and misfortune were linked with things,
gain and loss came to be in the mind,
they formed parties and cabals,
and contentious speech battered one another.
In ancient times, the heroes of Great Qí,
the men of the Three Jìn,
would at times close their eyes and bare their chests,
distinguishing one from another,
all taking the hundred-year lifespan as hard to obtain,
and the passing of sun and moon as changeable;
all harnessed strong horses,
prepared fine clothing,
admired pearls and jade,
adorned their tapestries and walls,
went out to flatter their lords and superiors,
came home to deceive fathers and elder brothers,
affected sharpness and intelligence,
competed and raced in every direction,
houses were ruined by clever sons,
states perished because of talented ministers,
thus they did not finish out their natural years but cut themselves off and joined bustle with the world.
Therefore, the tree in the mountain,
though great at root, is never harmed.
A myriad holes resound in harmony,
and suddenly all is finished.
If the wild goose no longer survives,
and its substance is lost, then only turbid-patterns remain;
if death and life have no difference,
yet the tortoise may be made a treasure,
one knows fortune and misfortune.
Therefore, the perfected one purifies his substance and clouds his form,
death and life unchanged and never has a word.
Those who distinguish words
hold to discourse about the Way;
those who break off arguments
open the beginning of destroying virtue;
those who apportion energies
create illness in themselves;
those with two minds
create troubles in all things.
Therefore, those who ornament the harness on their horses
travel and lack true support;
those whose thoughts rest on success and failure
sit and seek opponents;
those who cross barriers and attack fortresses
are people of Zhào;
those who lift mountains and fill seas
are people of Yān and Chǔ.
When Zhuāng Zhōu saw all this,
he thus recounted the mysteries of Way and Virtue,
explained the root of non-action,
used allegory to broaden it,
borrowed things to extend it,
merely to amuse the heart of non-action and wander freely through the world;
how could he have wished to seek the gates of Xiányáng and vie in argument with Jìxià?
Those who are good at connecting with others
only guide them,
never oppose them.
Thus, when Gōng Mèng Jìzǐ came dressed in embroidery,
Mòzǐ did not attack him;
when Zhōngshān Zǐmóu had his heart set upon the palace of Wèi,
Zhānzǐ did not reject him.
Follow the cause of their coming,
use the means by which they arrive,
go along and accord with them,
let them settle themselves,
draw them out and open them,
let them stretch themselves.
As for the book of Zhuāng Zhōu—how could it be worth much discussion!
He has yet to hear of the discourse of the Great Beginning,
or the subtle words of the mysterious ancients!
Simply be able not to harm things and let physical form live,
things suffer no damage and spirit becomes clear,
body and spirit reside within, and Way and Virtue are perfected,
loyalty and trust do not depart, and all is balanced above and below.
Thus, what is uttered now continues the ancient,
though the words are equal, their meaning differs;
thus, the heart can safeguard its root,
but what the mouth utters need not be interdependent.”
Then, those two and three disciples,
buffeted by wind and tossed by waves,
looked at each other, their pulses racing,
lost order and withdrew,
stumbling and losing their steps.
Following behind and watching them,
those behind their ears mostly understood the same,
knowing they were empty and dispirited, and ashamed before the aged recluse.

“Discourse on Music.”
Liú Zǐ asked,
“Kǒngzǐ said:
‘For securing those above and governing the people,
nothing excels lǐ;
for transforming customs and changing habits,
nothing excels yuè.’
Now, as for lǐ—
it is by lǐ that men and women are distinguished,
fathers and sons are completed,
rulers and ministers are established,
and the common people are brought to peace;
among the tools of governance, none ranks before this,
thus for securing those above and governing the people, nothing excels lǐ.
Now, gold, stone, silk, and bamboo—the sounds of bells, drums, pipes, and strings;
shields, axes, feathers, and yak-tails—the deportments of advancing, retreating, bowing, and looking up—
of what benefit are these to government if present?
Of what harm to transformation are they if absent?
And yet it is said that, for transforming customs and changing habits, nothing excels yuè?”
Master Ruǎn replied:
“Excellent!
This question of yours.
Formerly, Kǒngzǐ recorded only the essentials,
but had not yet set forth the broad outline.
Now, I will discuss the main lines for you,
and you may prepare the details yourself.”
“Now, as for yuè,
it is the embodiment of Heaven and Earth,
the nature of the myriad things.
When their forms are united,
and their natures are attained,
then there is harmony;
when their forms are separated,
and their natures are lost,
then there is estrangement.
In ancient times, when the Sage created yuè,
he sought to follow the nature of Heaven and Earth,
and embody the generation of the myriad things.
Thus he determined the pitches of Heaven and Earth at the eight directions,
in order to receive the sounds of the eight winds of yīn and yáng.
He equalized them by the pitch of Huángzhōng, the note of balance,
to open the emotions and vital energies of all living things.
Thus, when lǜ and lǚ harmonize, yīn and yáng are in concord;
when the sounds are appropriate, all things find their kind;
men and women do not leave their proper place,
rulers and ministers do not violate their stations;
throughout the Four Seas there is unity of vision,
and the Nine Provinces have the same rhythm.
When played at the Round Altar, the spirits of Heaven descend;
when played at the Square Mountains, the spirits of Earth respond above.
When Heaven and Earth are united in virtue, the myriad things are united in their generation,
reward and punishment need not be used, and the people are at peace.”
“Qián and Kūn are simple and easy;
thus, yǎyuè is not excessive.
Dào and dé are calm and bland;
thus, there is neither sound nor flavor.
When not excessive, yīn and yáng flow naturally;
when without flavor, all things find joy by themselves.
Day by day, transformation toward good is achieved without awareness;
customs and habits are altered and become one with this yuè.
This is the dào of nature,
the origin of yuè.”
“Later, when sages no longer arose,
dào and dé grew neglected and decayed;
governance and law were unsettled,
cleverness stirred up things,
transformation declined and desires were active,
and each had its own customs.
Thus, the teachings invented by individual masters were called ‘winds’;
when practiced and enacted, these were called ‘customs.’
The wind of Chǔ and Yuè values bravery,
thus their customs take life lightly;
the wind of Zhèng and Wèi values licentiousness,
thus their customs are frivolous.
Because they take life lightly,
there arise songs of leaping into fire or water;
because they are frivolous,
there are tunes like Sāngxián and Púshàng.
Each sings what it desires,
each chants what it does,
those who yearn for it weep,
those who hear it sigh,
and when one turns and leaves it,
none are not filled with emotion.
Cherishing the pleasure of long days,
embracing the lament of long nights,
gathering together and harmonizing,
forming groups and practicing,
endlessly without ceasing,
abandoning the affection of father and son,
loosening the regulations of ruler and minister,
depleting the lǐ of households,
abandoning the occupation of farming,
forgetting the lasting joys of life,
and exalting customs of licentious indulgence.
Thus, to the south of Jiānghuái the people delight in cruelty,
between Zhāng and Rǔ the people delight in flight,
Wú has the ritual of twin swords,
Zhào has the guests who hold the qín.
When emotion stirs within,
the sound enters the ear,
hands and feet leap and soar,
and one is not aware of the shock.”
“Those who value bravery offend those above,
those who are dissolute abandon kinship.
To offend those above is to make ruler and minister oppose each other;
to abandon kinship is to alienate father and son.
When alienation and opposition intermix,
trouble and calamity arise.
When disaster begins, intentions diverge;
when worries arise, concerns are not aligned.
Thus, the eight directions have different winds;
the Nine Provinces have diverse customs;
estrangement and division occur,
none can communicate with each other.
Their sounds differ, their energies separate;
their tunes and rhythms are not aligned.
Therefore, the sage establishes harmonizing notes,
sets up balanced sounds,
regulates rituals appropriate to the occasion,
establishes deportment in accordance with compliance,
so that those who play yuè under Heaven all take it as their model.
From high to low,
with appropriate gradations,
until reaching the common people,
all hear it.
The songs and ballads chant the virtue of former kings,
those who bow and rise learn the bearing of former kings,
vessels and instruments imitate the models of former kings,
measures and numbers accord with the system of former kings;
it enters the heart,
permeates the energies,
when heart and energy are in harmony,
then customs become uniform.”
“When the sages established the deportments of advance, retreat, bow, and gaze,
it was to bend the body,
and submit the mind,
to facilitate what is cultivated,
and bring ease to what is served.
The singing and chanting of poetry and tunes,
is to express harmony and peace,
and make manifest what is not attained.
The bells and drums serve to regulate hearing,
the feathers and yak-tails serve to regulate sight,
the listeners do not become unbalanced,
the viewers do not become fatigued;
when ears and eyes are not unbalanced or fatigued, customs are transformed and changed:
thus, for transforming customs and altering habits, nothing excels yuè.
Thus the eight tones have their essential forms,
the five notes have their natural qualities,
and those of the same kind are balanced by relative size.
Since they have natural qualities,
they cannot be confused;
since those of the same kind are balanced by size,
they can be harmonized.
For example, the qín of Kōngsāng,
the sǐ of Yúnhé,
the pipe of Gūzhú,
and the chimes of Sìbīn,
all these are made of well-proportioned and pure-harmonized materials,
so that their sounds are mutually fitting,
and therefore must have fixed positions;
balanced by size,
they respond to the breath of Huángzhōng,
and therefore must have fixed numbers.
With fixed positions,
their instruments are valued and esteemed;
with fixed numbers,
their systems are not arbitrary.
Being esteemed,
they can be used to serve the spirits;
being not arbitrary,
they can be used to transform people.
Their materials resemble the images of Heaven and Earth,
so they must not be made capriciously;
their general sound resembles distant objects,
so they must not be altered at will.
Yǎ and Sòng have their distinctions,
thus human and divine are not mingled;
rhythms and gatherings have their numbers,
thus twists and turns are not disordered;
circles and turns have their measures,
thus bowing and looking up are not confused;
singing and chanting have their themes,
thus speech is not contradicted.
Guiding with goodness,
soothing with harmony,
guarding with what is central,
maintaining it with perseverance;
dispersing what is excessive,
adjusting its patterns,
supporting what is short-lived,
helping what is long-lived,
so as to eliminate the partial habits of custom,
and return to the great transformation of the sage kings.”
“When the former kings created music,
it was to regulate the dispositions of all things
and to unify the will of the world.
Therefore, they made its sounds harmonious,
and its expressions gentle.
Those below did not crave the sounds above;
the lord harbored no desire for the expressions of his ministers;
thus, upper and lower did not contend, and loyalty and righteousness were accomplished.
Proper music
serves to keep away licentious sounds;
thus, when music falls into neglect, licentious sounds arise.
Hàn Ài Dì cared little for proper music,
abolished and reduced the Music Bureau,
but did not know how to establish proper rituals;
the laws of music were left uncorrected,
and licentious sounds then emerged.
Zhāng Fàng and Chún Yú Cháng grew excessively arrogant and unrestrained,
Bǐng Qiáng and Jǐng Wǔ amassed extraordinary wealth in their age.
After the abolishment of music,
the common people grew ever more unruly and wanton.
As for those whose conduct was already not good and whose licentiousness became still more extreme,
it was because ritual was not properly established.”
“Punishment and instruction are one body;
ritual and music
are outer and inner.
If punishments are slack, teaching cannot be upheld alone;
if ritual is neglected, music has no foundation on which to stand.
There must be distinctions in rank and station,
a hierarchy between upper and lower—
this is called ritual;
when people are secure in their lives,
their feelings and thoughts are without sorrow—
this is called music.
Carriages and attire, banners and flags, palaces and mansions, food and drink—
these are the implements of ritual;
bells and chimes, drums and tabors, qín and sè, singing and dancing—
these are the instruments of music.
If ritual exceeds its bounds, distinctions of rank and status are confused;
if music loses its proper sequence, closeness and distance become disorderly.
Ritual regulates appearances;
music brings harmony to the heart;
ritual governs the exterior,
music transforms the interior;
when ritual and music are correct, the world is at peace.”
“In the past, when the people of Wèi sought ornate tassels and curved bell frames, Kǒngzǐ sighed,
for he lamented the destruction of ritual and the collapse of music.
Now, the bell is the master of sound;
the frame is the form for the bell.
When a bell loses its form, its sound loses its master;
when master and form have no constancy, strange sounds arise together.
In eras of rise and decline,
the changes of ancient and modern seem as one;
therefore, when the teachings of the sages fall into ruin, clever people all create peculiar music.
Jǐng Wáng delighted in the tonal system of the great bells;
Píng Wáng enjoyed the songs of Shī Yán;
the nobles and ministers clapped their hands in admiration;
the common people eagerly wished to hear;
proper music was then abandoned,
Zhèng sounds flourished,
the poems of Yǎ and Sòng were no longer recited,
and bewitching and licentious tunes were sought instead.
Yán Nián composed the ‘Song of Overthrowing the City,’
and Xiào Wǔ longed for beautiful and flirtatious women;
Yōng Mén created the music of the pines and cypresses,
Mǐn Wáng remembered wearing thin clothing before the cold had ended.
Thus, when the sounds of melancholy and languor arise,
and words of grievance and discontent become prevalent,
then later generations harbor thoughts of indulgence and extravagance,
and people are inwardly self-serving;
this is why the gentleman detests the ‘Song of Great Overpowering’
and loathes the dance of ‘Běi Lǐ.’”
“In olden times, the former kings established music
not to indulge the eyes and ears,
nor to elevate the pleasures of hidden chambers.
Rather, it was to harmonize the energies of Heaven and Earth,
to quiet the spirits of all things;
to secure the positions of high and low,
and to establish the true nature of fate.
Thus, the songs of the Pure Temple praised accomplished deeds,
the banquet odes extolled the virtues of ritual and deference;
the people were thereby transformed toward goodness,
and even those of foreign customs admired their virtue;
this is why licentious sounds were rare,
and proper music valued.”
“Yet ritual changes with circumstances,
and music is adapted to the times;
so the Five Emperors had different standards,
and each of the Three Kings created uniquely;
not because they contradicted one another,
but because they responded to the needs of their era.
When the people become at ease with licentious music,
and break down the former kings’ rectitude,
later kings must create new music,
each proclaiming their merit and virtue to the world,
communicating these changes so the people do not grow weary.
Yet only the names and forms are altered,
the songs and chants adapted,
but as for the sound of music,
its harmony and balance remain unchanged;
so Huáng Dì sang the divine ‘Yún Mén,’
Shǎo Hào chanted the traces of the phoenix-bird;
even as the names of ‘Xián Chí’ and ‘Liù Yīng’ changed,
the scale of Huáng Zhōng remained unaltered.
Therefore, those who are versed in the Way can judge music properly,
but those who merely love pleasing sounds are not fit to discuss its laws.”
“Shùn ordered Kuí to be Director of Music,
teaching the imperial offspring the virtue of perfect harmony:
‘The Shī express purpose,
chants express words,
sounds follow the chant,
pitch harmonizes sound.
When the eight tones are attuned,
none overpowers the others,
and spirit and man are in harmony.’
It is also said:
‘I would hear the six lǜ, five sounds, and eight tones,
all alive in governance,
and thus produce the five utterances.
Attend and listen!’
Now, confusing the hands in licentious music
drowns mind and ear,
thus losing harmony and balance—
the gentleman does not listen.
It is said that proper music is accessible, serene, and simple;
the heart is clear and the energy pure;
one thus perceives music,
and so produces correct utterances.
Kuí said:
‘Striking and clanging the sounding jade,
striking the qín and sè and chanting aloud,
the spirits of the ancestors arrive;
the noble guests are in their places,
the assembled lords are yielding in virtue;
below, the pipes and drums resound,
the chorus, chant, and wood percussion are all in concert,
the shēng and bells add a tranquil air,
the birds and beasts frolic in delight;
the xiāo and sháo music is performed in nine sequences,
and the phoenix descends in stately form.’
Kuí said:
‘As for me, when I strike stones and clap stones together,
all the wild creatures dance in unison,
and the various attendants are perfectly in accord.’
The Shī expresses purpose,
chanting expresses words;
grasping chimes and striking the qín,
following the pitch according to law,
recount the virtues of the former kings,
so the ancestral spirits are summoned;
the shēng and bells add calm,
proper music is gentle and rare,
when governance is excellent without harm,
thus creatures multiply and flourish;
when music has its proper rhythm,
and nine sequences are completed,
yin and yang are harmonized,
harmony pervades,
thus distant birds arrive in stately form;
plain, not ornate,
the four corners of the world are united,
thus beating stones together,
all creatures dance;
it is said that when the world is at peace,
all things find their place,
sounds and music are not clamorous,
tranquil, without sign or omen,
so all officials are united in harmony.
Thus, when Kǒngzǐ was in Qí and heard the sháo music,
he did not notice the taste of meat for three months,
which expresses that the highest music causes one to lose all desire,
heart and breath tranquil and even,
so that even meat is not thought savory.
Considering this,
one knows that the joy of the sage is nothing but harmony.”
“From the music of Xīlíng and Qīngyáng, all was taken from bamboo;
listening to the song of the fènghuáng,
revering the image of the elder wind,
drawing upon the great forests,
that which people of the time had not seen,
and what the common people had rarely heard—
therefore, all under Heaven cherished its virtue and were transformed by its spirit.
When yǎyuè pervades the Zhōu, then the myriad things are in harmony;
when its essence is tranquil, listening is not excessive;
when it is simple and easy, it regulates and commands the spirit;
when it is calm and solemn, it subdues people’s hearts.
This is the intention with which the former kings created music.
But as later generations declined and music was made in decay,
its materials were no longer genuine,
its instruments no longer solid,
its structures lacked integrity,
it was drawn from common things,
identical to what was among the people,
each seeking only what pleased them,
indulging whatever remained in their passions;
the sounds of the lanes vied in pitch,
the music of the deep alleys contended to be first;
children gathered to sing of wealth and honor,
shepherds and cowherds bore burdens as they sang of poverty and lowliness.
Though the offices of ruler and minister were not yet abolished,
one man still harbored ten thousand hearts.”
“At the end of the era of Xiàhòu,
ten thousand girls were gathered,
dressed in embroidered garments,
fed with grain and meat,
singing in chorus at dawn,
and those who heard it felt distress and sorrow;
all under Heaven suffered from its disasters,
and the common people were wounded by its poison.
In the late period of the Yīn rulers,
this sort of music was also performed,
there were wine pools and forests of meat,
banqueting by night and by day;
yet the sound of lamentation had not ceased,
and the neighboring states had already seized their qín and sè instruments.
Drinking wine throughout the hall,
with music performed, they wept and shed tears;
if not all were sorrowful,
then this was not true music.
In the time when Wáng Jūchén was in office,
new music was performed in the ancestral temple,
yet all who heard it wept in grief.
When Huán Dì heard the Chǔ qín,
he was so sorrowful and pained at heart,
that, leaning on his armrest, he mourned,
letting out a long, melancholy sigh, saying:
‘Excellent indeed!
With such a qín,
having just one is already enough.’
When Shùn Dì visited Gōnglíng,
passing Fánqú,
he heard birds singing and was saddened,
tears streaming sideways,
saying:
‘How lovely the birds sing!’
He bade his attendants chant it,
saying:
‘If the sound of the strings were thus,
would it not be joyful indeed?’
This, then, is to take sorrow as joy.
Truly, if one takes sorrow as joy,
then what delight can there be left in all under Heaven?
If there is no joy in the world,
yet there is harmony between yīn and yáng,
and disasters do not arise,
even this is difficult enough.
Music,
is what causes people’s spirits to become balanced and harmonious,
preventing withering energies from entering,
bringing Heaven and Earth into concord,
so that distant beings gather together;
therefore it is called music.
But now it moves people to tears,
exhausts and hurts their vitality,
disturbs the balance of cold and heat,
causes things to be unfulfilled;
even if string and bamboo are played,
it ought to be called lamentation;
how could one, sighing deeply and looking down, call this music!
In the past, Jì Liúzǐ played the qín facing the wind,
and those who listened wept, soaking their lapels with tears.
His disciple said:
‘How wonderful the qín playing!
Truly marvelous it is.’
Jì Liúzǐ said:
‘Music is praised as good,
lamentation as hurtful;
what I have played is sorrowful and hurtful,
not good music.’
To speak thus,
strings and bamboo need not necessarily be called music,
and singing and chanting are not always good;
thus Mòzǐ condemned music.
Alas!
Those who take mourning as joy,
why did Hú Pìxuán immerse himself in grief and never change,
and so wished to become a commoner?
Why did Lǐ Sī follow sorrow and never return,
and so desired to chase the cunning hare?
Alas!
Can the gentleman not take warning from this?”

He spoke of the beginning of Heaven and Earth,
referring to the deeds of Shénnóng and Huáng Dì—
all was luminous and clear.
No one knows how many years he lived.
He once dwelled on Sūmén Mountain,
so later ages all called him Xián.
He cultivated his nature and prolonged his life,
shining together with nature itself,
and regarded what Yáo and Shùn served as if it were something held in his own palm.
He considered ten thousand li as a single step,
and a thousand years as a single morning.
He traveled without haste and stayed without remaining,
sought the Great Way without anywhere to dwell.
The Master responded to change and submitted to harmony,
took Heaven and Earth as his home,
and when circumstance waned, stood tall and alone;
believing himself capable of keeping pace with creation,
changing and transforming along with it,
and thus he silently sought after the Way and Virtue,
not aligning himself with the age.
Those who preferred their own ways criticized him; the ignorant were suspicious of him,
not understanding the transformations and mysterious subtlety;
but the Master did not change his course on account of worldly blame or suspicion.
The Master regarded the Central Plains in the world as not even as significant as flies and mosquitoes on a curtain;
so in the end he never regarded it as a concern,
but exhausted his thoughts on strange and foreign lands,
wandering and observing their music,
such as the world had never seen,
roaming endlessly without termination.
He left his writings on Sūmén Mountain and departed,
and no one under Heaven knew where he had gone.
Someone sent a letter to Dàrén xiānshēng, saying:
“Of all things honored under Heaven,
none are more esteemed than the jūnzǐ:
their dress has a constant color,
their appearance has a constant regulation,
their speech has fixed measure,
their conduct has standard forms;
when standing, they are bowed like a musical chime,
their hands folded as if embracing a drum,
their movements and stillness are measured,
their pace matches the shāng and yǔ modes,
whether advancing, retreating, turning—
all have pattern and rule.
Their heart is as if harboring ice,
always cautious and trembling,
constraining their body and cultivating themselves,
more and more careful by the day,
choosing well where to go,
fearing only to be lost,
reciting the inherited teachings of Zhōu and Kǒng,
praising the virtue of Táng and Yú,
cultivating only according to the law,
conquering themselves only by ritual,
holding jade tablets in their hands,
keeping their feet upon cord and ink-line,
making their conduct a present inspection,
making their words the standard for inconceivable time;
in youth they are praised by villagers,
when grown they are known in the state,
wishing to plan for the rank of Sāngōng above,
at the least not losing the post of provincial governor,
so they carry gold and jade,
let tassels of brocade hang down,
enjoy an honored position,
receive fief and lands,
let their fame resound in later generations,
make merit and virtue equal to the ancients;
they serve rulers,
tend the commoners,
when retired manage their household,
nurture wife and sons,
divine for fortune before settling,
plan the fullness of blessings,
keep disaster far and fortune near,
ever firm and secure themselves:
this is truly the high aspiration of scholar-gentlemen,
the beautiful conduct unchanged from antiquity to the present.
But now, sir, you have let your hair hang loose and live in the midst of the vast sea,
far from such as those called jūnzǐ;
I fear the world may sigh over you yet criticize you.
Your conduct is laughed at by the age,
your person has no way to reach out on its own;
that may be called shameful indeed.
To live in a place of hardship
and yet be mocked by the world for your conduct—
I, for you, do not approve.”
Thereupon, Dàrén xiānshēng sighed gently and
responded as if borrowing the clouds and rainbows, saying:
“What connection can there be with such words!
For the true Dàrén
shares essence with the Creator,
coming forth with Heaven and Earth,
roaming freely through the world,
maturing together with the Dào,
ever-changing and dispersing or gathering,
never fixed in form.
Heaven and Earth lay out bounds within,
while their floating clarity opens and reaches beyond;
the enduring solidity of Heaven and Earth
is something the common world cannot match.
I shall explain it for you:
In the past,
Heaven was once below,
Earth once above,
overturned and reversed,
never yet secure and firm—
how could anything keep its pattern and constancy then?
Heaven moved because of Earth,
mountains sank, rivers rose,
clouds scattered, thunder destroyed,
the universe lost order;
how then could you choose your ground on which to walk,
or pace to shāng and yǔ’s rhythm?
In the past, the vital energies wrestled for survival,
the myriad things met only death and worry,
the limbs would not obey,
bodies became earth and mud,
roots pulled out, branches torn—
all lost their place;
how could you then constrain your body and cultivate yourself,
bow like a chime, embrace like a drum?
Lǐ Mù achieved merit but met death,
Bó Zhōng was loyal but his family line ended,
seeking advantage brought ruin to themselves,
seeking rank and reward brought extinction to their house;
how then could you clutch piles of gold and jade,
faithfully serve your Lord yet preserve wife and sons?
Have you not seen how lice dwell inside the hem of breeches,
hiding deep in seams, lurking in rotted cotton,
thinking themselves to have a fine home?
They dare not stray from the seam,
nor move beyond the crotch of the cloth,
thinking themselves to be on the cord and ink-line.
Hungry, they bite men,
thinking themselves to have endless food.
Yet when fire blazes and flames spread,
all cities and capitals are destroyed,
and all the lice die within the breeches, unable to escape.
How is your jūnzǐ, living within society’s bounds, any different from the lice dwelling in breeches?
How sad!
Yet you presume to say you keep disaster far, fortune near,
security everlasting;
also consider how the sun-bird soars beyond the dust, while the wren plays among reeds and water-shields,
the great and small truly do not encroach upon each other;
so how could such as your jūnzǐ be compared to me?
Moreover, recently the Xià perished to the Shāng,
Zhōu was scattered by Liú,
Gěng and Bó became ruins,
Fēng and Hào turned into hills,
the perfected sage visits once and dynasties repay one another,
yet their dwellings never stay,
and others possess them,
your fiefs and lands—
with whom will they endure long?
Thus, the perfected man does not abide by residence,
is not ruled by cultivation,
takes sun and moon for regulation,
takes yīn and yáng for timing.
How would he long for favor in human affairs,
or be bound by the times?
Following the eastern clouds,
riding the western wind,
with yīn defends the female’s stillness,
with yáng claims the male’s might,
his will follows what he desires,
nothing can constrain him;
so how could he fail to manifest himself, or fear the laughter of the world?”
“In former times, when Heaven and Earth separated,
the myriad things were born together;
the great ones contented themselves within their nature,
the small ones maintained composure in form;
yīn hid its vital energy,
yáng issued its essence;
no harm needed to be avoided,
no benefit sought to be won;
when let go, nothing was lost,
when gathered in, nothing was excessive.
Death came not as premature,
life not for length;
fortune could not be obtained,
disaster had no one to blame:
each followed their fated lot,
keeping to their own measure.
The enlightened did not rely on cleverness to win,
nor the ignorant rely on dullness to lose;
the weak were not pressed by fear,
nor the strong exhausted their strength.
Thus, even without rulers, the many things settled in order,
without ministers, all affairs found their pattern,
maintaining their bodies and cultivating their natures,
never straying from their proper course;
only through this,
could long endurance be achieved.
But now you create music to disorder true sound,
invent colors to deceive in form;
outwardly alter appearances,
inwardly conceal intentions,
harboring desires to pursue abundance,
using deceit and falsity to pursue reputation;
when rulers are established, tyranny arises,
when ministers are positioned, treachery is born,
sitting to devise rites and laws,
binding and shackling the common people,
cheating the simple and deluding the unsophisticated,
hoarding wisdom as personal divinity,
the strong encroach on the weak and oppress them,
the weak become withered and serve others,
pretending to integrity in order to achieve greed,
harboring danger within and showing outward kindness,
when crimes are at hand, refusing to repent,
when fortune comes, growing self-important,
riding this to pursue favor and clearance,
thus stagnation is repeated and never overcome.”
If there is no nobility, then the lowly do not harbor resentment;
if there is no wealth, then the poor do not contend;
each is content within himself and has nothing to seek.
When favor has nowhere to return,
then death and defeat have no object for vengeance;
when strange sounds do not arise, the ear is not led to crave listening,
when wanton beauty is not revealed, the eye does not alter its gaze;
when the ear and eye do not entice and change each other, there is nothing to disorder the mind;
this was how people in former ages reached their stopping place.
Now you honor the worthy to boast over each other,
compete in ability to surpass each other,
vie for power to rule over one another,
lavish favor and nobility to outdo each other,
drive all under Heaven to strive after these things—
this is why superiors and inferiors mutually destroy each other.
Exhausting the utmost of Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things to serve insatiable desires for sights and sounds—
this is not the way to nurture the people.
Therefore you fear the people will see through this.
Thus you bestow heavy rewards to delight them,
enforce harsh punishments to awe them;
wealth is depleted, and the rewards are not enough;
punishments are exhausted, and penalties are not enacted;
then at last comes the disaster of a ruined state, a slaughtered ruler, and scattering destruction.
Is this not the doing of you, the gentlemen?
The rules and rites of you gentlemen
are in truth but the arts of injuring, disordering, imperiling, and destroying the world;
yet you regard them as fine conduct and an immutable Way—
is this not excessive!
Now I wander carefree beyond Heaven and Earth,
taking Zàohuà as my friend,
in the morning breakfasting at Tānggǔ,
in the evening drinking from the Western Sea,
about to transform and shift with change,
to follow Dào from start to end—
is this not the truest fullness among the myriad things?
Therefore, he who does not understand what is natural is unfit to speak of Dào;
he who is dim to the shining is unfit to discuss clarity:
this refers to you."
After the teacher had made his pronouncement,
those who delight in the strange under Heaven marveled at it,
and the indignant praised it as lofty.
They did not know its substance,
nor see its truth,
and guessed at its Way with doubtful ears;
attaching names full of falsehood,
none recognized its reality,
nor comprehended its sense.
Though they called it wondrous and lofty,
among those for whom it was not strange as before,
there was nothing to it.
The perfect man
does not know his own nobility,
does not appear as spiritual,
the way to spirit and nobility exists within,
while the myriad things revolve externally;
thus, all under Heaven comes to an end without knowing its purpose.
Far away, in the wilds where Fúyáo rises, there was a hermit who, seeing this, rejoiced,
believing himself equal in aspiration and walking the same path, and he said:
"How fine!
In seeing it now, my frustrated feelings are eased.
The pure and honest Way of the high antiquity has already been lost,
and the trivial outgrowths and remaining adornments rise together.
Jackals and tigers are greedy and cruel,
all beings are guiltless,
but harm is taken as profit,
their natures destroyed, their bodies lost,
I cannot bear to see this,
and so I have left and dwell here.
People are not fit to be companions,
it is better to have wood and stone as neighbors.
Ānqī fled to Péngshān,
Jiǎolǐ hid in Dānshuǐ,
Bào Jiāo stood in withered austerity,
Lái Wéi departed and died afar;
so it is for me too!
I will exalt my will and make it manifest,
and thus end my life here.
Birds live and beasts die,
burying their forms and leaving their bones,
never returning to what they once were in life again!
Those whose wills accord seek each other out,
those who take pleasure in harmony come together;
with you, Master, do I share this."
Then the teacher let forth a rainbow to shield the dust,
tilted a cover of snow to hide the brightness,
leaned on a jade balustrade and wandered about,
gathered up all the reins and rode on serenely,
turning, he said to him:
"The True Man of Tàichū,
is the root of Heaven,
concentrates his breath and directs his intent,
so the myriad things exist.
When retreating, he does not see what is behind;
advancing, he does not glimpse what is ahead;
emerging in the northwest, he sets the pattern,
opening in the southeast, he makes a gate,
his subtle Way and virtue endure for ages delighting in themselves,
spanning Heaven and Earth and dwelling in honor.
In this way is my body made complete,
thus I do not avoid things but live among them,
and what I see is peaceful;
not burdened by things,
where I go afar is fulfillment;
roaming freely is enough to set my mind at ease,
soaring swiftly is enough to satisfy my heart.
Therefore the perfect man has no fixed dwelling,
Heaven and Earth are his lodging;
the perfect man has no master,
Heaven and Earth are his domain;
the perfect man has no tasks,
Heaven and Earth are his affairs;
he makes no distinction of right or wrong,
no difference of good and evil;
thus all under Heaven is covered by his grace, and myriad things thus flourish.
But as for hating others and liking oneself,
asserting self and condemning others,
rousing anger to strive and gain,
valuing will and slighting the body,
so birds live while beasts die—
what glory then is gained and revealed?
How sorrowful!
This is how you have used your mind!
Pursuing empty comfort and gain, you forget your own life,
seeking reputation, you lose your body,
indeed you differ in no way from those over there,
yet you dry up and die afar.
How is what you value even worth discussing?
I shall leave you now."
Thereupon he raised his eyebrows and swept his eyes afar,
shook his sleeves and stroked his robe,
made the reins slack and let the horse go free,
then the wind rose and the clouds soared.
That man gazed after him, tears falling,
lamenting his own purpose,
clothed in tree bark,
dwelling beneath the rocks,
fearing he would not live to the end of the night.
The master passed by the Divine Palace and rested,
rinsed his mouth with the Wú spring and walked on,
turned toward Yōu and wandered, sightseeing there.
He saw someone carrying firewood on a hill,
and sighed, saying:
“How will you end with this?”
The woodcutter said:
“Whether this will be my end
or not,
moreover, the sage harbors no fixed thoughts;
why be so mournful?
For the flourishing and decline, change and transformation,
never stand still in this world.
Store one’s ability within oneself,
hide it and wait for the times.
Sūn, even after his foot was cut off, could still capture Páng;
Suī rested only after his ribs were broken;
Bǎilǐ suffered hardship and yet served as prime minister to Yíng;
Yá, though old, aided Zhōu;
after complete ruin they returned again,
always suffering want first and gathering merit later.
Qín overthrew the six kingdoms,
united and absorbed their territories,
exterminated the feudal lords,
sat facing south, calling himself Emperor,
so elegant in beauty,
so proud of splendor and luxury,
chiseling through the southern mountains to make gates,
marking out the Eastern Sea as a door,
with ten thousand chambers endlessly following one another,
hoping to preserve infinity forever,
beautifying palaces and lavish canopies,
striking bells and drums to display his music,
expanding parks and deepening pools,
rising north of the Wèi to build Xiányáng.

weary, soon to turn east again.
Departures and gatherings are like clouds and mist,
coming and going like the swirling wind.
Wealth and honor belong to the space between bowing and looking up,
why assume poverty and lowliness are to be forever?
Liú Hóu rose from among defeated captives,
wielding power, subduing wild lands;
Zhào Píng was enfeoffed with Dōnglíng,
yet one morning became a commoner.
Branches and leaves entrust themselves to the root,
the passage between life and death is the same as that between prosperity and decline;
attaining one’s aspiration, one rises with fate,
losing momentum, one falls with the times.

change pushing change along;
blessing and misfortune have no fixed master,

why should the carrier of firewood lament?”
The master, hearing this,

the stars fall, the sun and moon decline,
soaring upward, what longing have I!
Garments are not layered, yet the raiment is fine,
the sash unornamented but shines by itself,
above and below I wander—who can recognize my constancy?
Thus I go away and drift afar,
ride the clouds at will,
raise a canopy of vital energy,
wandering and circling beyond all vastness.
Erect the long star as my banner,
beat thunder and lightning as my drum,
open Bùzhōu Mountain and send forth my chariot,
striding in ease across all nine wilds.
Sitting in the center of the land looking back once,
gazing at High Peaks to journey on;
I hold my pure conduct and raise my banner,
letting my mind ride far beyond the frontiers.
Those who chose the former path but did not cultivate it,
sped blindly on and only grew more remote,
casting off the multitude of worldly tasks,
how could trivial matters be worth reliance?
Lightening the form to rise easily,
subtle and mysterious, the spirit grows full.
Command Yí Yì to slacken the sun,
summon Xīn Lái to slow the winds.
Grasp the long boughs of Fúsāng,
climb the soaring spiral to towering heights.
Leap through darkness like the drifting wind,
bathe in the brilliance of shining light.
Abandon robes, but not wear them,
wear clouds and vital breath as my garb on the journey.

at dusk rest my steed by Chángquán,
at times visit Yānzī and change my vital energy,
shining bright as flowers to illuminate the dark.
Raise my banner left at Zhūyáng,
erect my flag right at Xuán Yīn,
alter appearances, change my course,
then soar secretly on my long journey.
Yang and Yin alternate and keep moving,
the four seasons rush by each in turn.
Only the transformation of the immortals is so suddenly swift,
my heart delights not in lingering long.
A startled wind stirs but leaves behind joy,
though clouds arise, my worries are forgotten.
Sudden lightning fades and spirit roams free,
traversing the vast expanse, drifting afar.

penetrating heart and spirit,
soaring far off into untold vastness,
my heart goes forth and forgets to return,

summoning the Jade Maidens of Great Darkness,
greeting the fairest of the kings above,
their bodies flow in unrestrained vapor,
wearing the pure quintessence as their true adornment,
harmonies of delight with subtle transmission,
first fragrant beauty flushing like spirits,
splendid charm blazing forth together,
gleaming colors shining bright side by side,
trailing black hair and drooping side-locks,
cheeks glowing red and ever renewed.
The hour dims and all will pass,
wind flutters by and stirs my robe.
The vapor parts and mist dissipates,
haze scatters and returns eternally.
My heart is disoriented and thoughts roam,
my gaze turns but never dries.
Raising pure breeze as my pennon,
circling and returning, turning again.
Rising through blazing sun, passing beyond the bounds,
ordering Zhù Róng to drive it on.

floating, dazzling the dawn clouds.
Vast, boundless, with no place to rest,
aloof and matchless, I stand alone.

pity the earth below, how withered and worn.

how could it compare with such company?

girded with a circling Yáng-style sash,

inhaling floating mists,
dining on morning clouds and rosy haze,
rising with dawn clouds,
soaring on the spring wind,
vigorous to the east of Tàijí,
wandering to the west of Kūnlún.
He abandoned reins and let the whip fall,
casting sidelong glances at the capitals of Táng and Yú.

"Alas!
Time is not as valuable as years,
years not as valuable as Heaven,
Heaven not as valuable as the Dào,
and the Dào not as valuable as Spirit.
Spirit
is the root of what is natural.
Those who continually vie with each other believe themselves esteemed in the world;
but how do they know the world’s lowliness lies in this!
Thus, to compete with the world for honor—
honor is not enough to be called noble;
to compete with the world for wealth—
wealth is not enough to be esteemed first.
